subtopic: MR. FORTIN-CONVERSION OF COQUALEETZA HOSPITAL INTO COMMUNITY CENTRE
MR. FORTIN-CONVERSION OF COQUALEETZA HOSPITAL INTO COMMUNITY CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 24 last, I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) a number of questions concerning the conversion of the Coqualeetza Hospital into a community centre and the related family and social problems. The minister's answers to these questions are recorded on page 4566 of Hansard.
On March 24, the minister replied that no decision had been made as to the conversion of this property, further indicating that three proposals had been made by the Indians, that his department was studying each of
these proposals and that the government would make a decision later. May I quote the minister's words:
-We are not, however, in a position to give an answer at this time.
Now, the same day, Mr. Wilbur T. Campbell, president of the North American Indian Brotherhood of British Columbia and of the Coqualeetza Community Centre received a letter from Mr. Bergevin, Assistant Deputy Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, stating quite clearly that a decision had already been taken and would stand.
Mr. Speaker, I contend that the House has been misinformed, as I have been myself, and that this prevents us from making the representations that should be made at this level.
I, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That any decision be withheld until the conclusion of a thorough investigation regarding the conversion of the Coqualeetza Hospital into a community centre.

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY ON SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNOLOGICAL CO-OPERATION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minisler of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY ON SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNOLOGICAL CO-OPERATION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 41 (2), I should like to table, in the two official lan-

April 27, 1971
Trade Agreement with Germany guages, copies of an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the Federal Republic of Germany on scientific and technological co-operation.
Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege last week of leading a trade and industry mission to the Federal Republic of Germany. The mission was made up of 28 leading businessmen representing a wide range of interests, and a group of senior federal and provincial officials. Our purposes were 1) to sign this agreement, developed earlier by a science-technology mission of scientists and officials from business and government, 2) to develop closer economic relations of every type between Canada and the Federal Republic and 3) to discuss with the German government bilateral, European and multilateral trade problems.
This new scientific and technological agreement is similar to those with Belgium and the USSR which we have concluded this year. Its aims are to encourage the exchange of information and research; to facilitate the movement of scientists and technologists; and, through the exchange of knowledge and experience, to contribute to Canada's trade and industrial development and to the growth of our exports of advanced industrial products and services.
I might add that the science and technology mission had identified a number of areas of collaboration with Germany which are particularly promising for Canada- computer software, oceanography, geophysics, metallurgy, construction techniques, to name only a few.
The choice of business representatives on the mission I led was related to these promising areas for trade and development as well as other sectors of mutual interest. The business members of my mission travelled widely throughout Germany, for private meetings with manufacturers, bankers and prospective investors. They developed new contacts which are expected to lead to increased trade, to the introduction of new technology into Canada, to licensing agreements, joint ventures, new investment and to other forms of co-operation between the business communities of the two countries. The businessmen were well pleased with the opportunities the mission was able to develop. A detailed report on these opportunities is being prepared and will be released when it is completed.
While the meetings between business men were proceeding, I held discussions with the German Ministers and/or State Secretaries of Economics, Science, Foreign Affairs and Defence and their officials; and with the Governor of the German Central Bank.

Accompanied by members of'the mission, I also met with representatives of the Federation of German Industries, the German Chamber of Commerce and with a wide range of leading figures in the German business community. I encouraged them to step up their interest in the development of industry in Canada and in purchasing their basic food and material requirements from Canada, as well as in buying more of the products of our secondary industry. I also drew their attention to Canada
as a possible source of more of their energy needs in the future. World trading problems and prospects were quite extensively discussed, as well as Canadian policies on these important matters.
With ministers and officials I emphasized the problems which enlargement of the Common Market would bring to Canadian exporters to Britain.
I also spoke of the need to move forward at an early date toward a freer world trading environment. I sought to establish that the Federal Republic, as well as other members of the community, should in their own interests wish to undertake broad trade negotiations with outside countries as soon as practicable and generally avoid the disruption of established and valuable trade relations with Canada and other non-member countries.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these discussions were very useful. German ministers now have a better understanding and knowledge of the particular position of Canada in relation to the enlargement of the European Economic Community. I believe that they now better realize the extent of the mutuality of interest between Canada, the existing community and the prospective new members. German ministers emphasized repeatedly the commitment of their country to a multilateral free trading system.
I hope that this greater understanding will help to lead to better solutions of world trading problems, taking account of the interests of Canada and other trading partners of the Common Market. It would indeed be welcome if the EEC countries and the applicant members were prepared, in the coming months, to indicate their willingness to enter into another meaningful round of negotiations for the freeing of world trade.

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY ON SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNOLOGICAL CO-OPERATION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by thanking the minister for his usual courtesy in providing the opposition with a copy of his speech whenever he has the intention to make one on motions. This has proven to be most helpful.
We are indeed delighted that an agreement of this kind has been signed with the Federal Republic of Germany, a nation which has aroused the envy of the world, especially in the last decade, because of its economic and industrial aggressiveness. Certainly that country has much that we could copy and from which we could learn. One has only to visit Germany to be impressed at once by the psychology of its people who seem determined to make industrial progress. No day seems to be too long. There is one area in particular that we could emulate. Here is a country which over the past ten years has actually found it progressively more difficult to obtain enough employees to service its various economic projects and industrial complexes, while in Canada in the last ten years we seem to have been constantly fighting a losing battle to provide equal job opportunities and economic welfare.
The minister's statement speaks of the exchanges which will be possible between the business and scientific interests of the two nations. Up to now we only have the

April 27, 1971

signing of an agreement. Its success will depend on industry, the ambition of Canadian businessmen and technocrats, and the encouragement of the government in taking full advantage of the open door and the opportunities offered to us at this time. I hope the government will continue to take the lead in this regard and provide constant encouragement for these interests to take full advantage of the opportunity afforded to them.
I wish to deal with one other part of the statement. The statement deals with vague generalities. The minister spoke of his dealings and talks with ministers of the Federal Republic of Germany concerning the European Common Market and Canadian policies. I am sure they were in doubt about such policies because we in the Parliament of Canada are also in doubt.
We hope that at an early opportunity the minister will avail himself of the opportunity on motions to deal in some detail not only with the government's policies and programs with regard to the European Common Market but also the equally important subject of the government's position and progress toward freer international trade. This must be a complex problem as far as other nations are concerned in their dealings with Canada. In some areas we seem perfectly willing to progress rapidly toward a freer exchange of goods, but in other areas we are loath to reduce any tariff or non-tariff barriers in order to move toward a free exchange of goods between countries. The minister and the government should provide an opportunity for a full debate so that the opposition and the people of Canada will know to what degree the government's policy is directed toward free trade, whether it is a policy of selective free trade, progressive free trade or complete free trade. We in this country as well as the countries of the European Economic Community would like to know what the government's policy is in this regard.
The opposition welcomes the agreement that has been signed. This is real progress. We can learn much from the Federal Republic of Germany. We can gain much from its economic, industrial and technical know-how. I hope that country will find it equally lucrative to visit Canada.

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY ON SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNOLOGICAL CO-OPERATION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members always welcome reports of initiatives taken by the minister and his department in carrying on exchanges and discussions with responsible officials of other countries in an attempt to improve our economic relationships with those countries. These are certainly to be welcomed and encouraged. However, it should be pointed out that such initiatives will only achieve adequate results if they are cast within a proper and adequately thought-out policy framework, if, indeed, the objectives and the thrust of such initiatives are adequately defined. Members of this party have on many occasions pointed out to the government that we feel it has not adequately defined its policy objectives and the general thrust of its policy in encouraging trading relations with other countries.
Trade Agreement with Germany
One point that should also be noted is that, while I have no doubt that the 28 leading businessmen who accompanied the minister to Germany were all very well qualified in their own fields, I think it is to be regretted that representatives of the labour movement and of the agricultural industry were not included in the delegation. Representatives of these two groups could have added significantly to the usefulness of the mission.
I believe we will all agree that the signing of an agreement such as that described by the minister is useful and to be encouraged. However, by itself the agreement does not accomplish the objectives we would hope to achieve. Again, it is a matter of casting such agreements within a properly defined policy framework.
In addition, we should take note of the minister's statement that during the discussions with the German government and German businessmen he encouraged them to step up their interest in the development of industry in Canada and in the purchase of basic food and material requirements from Canada. Two points arise in this regard. First, what are the implications of the phrase "development of industry in Canada"? Does it simply mean we shall be obtaining more capital from Germany in future rather than from another country, or will such a move be properly related to whatever policy announcement the government may make with respect to foreign ownership of Canadian industries? Again, with respect to material requirements I notice the minister did not use the term "raw material requirements" though it seemed to me that the tone of his statement pointed in that direction. Everyone will agree that there is a need to encourage the export of agricultural and food products to Germany as well as to other countries in western Europe.
The minister also told us that discussions were held concerning world trading problems and prospects. It is, of course, essential and important to discuss this matter with other countries at every opportunity. The tone of the minister's statement certainly indicated the concern he now feels about the problems which are arising in consequence of the new developments in the European Economic Community. I believe we will agree with the minister that we should move toward a freer world trading environment, but I am sure the minister would also agree that there are many roadblocks in the way of achieving such an environment. Indeed, it is quite possible that such an environment may not be achieved by Canada and by other countries interested in such an objective. It is therefore essential that the government should have open to it alternative policy approaches designed to deal with possible problems that will arise in the future.
A good deal of publicity has been given in recent weeks to the development of world trading blocs and the problems which this is likely to create for countries such as Canada. The minister should be encouraged and, indeed, urged to deal with this situation and develop the approach of the department and of the government in this respect.
I also noted the minister's comment that it would indeed be welcome if the EEC countries and applicants
5256

April 27, 1971
Trade Agreement with Germany
were prepared to indicate their willingness to enter into further discussions. The words "it would indeed be welcome" suggest to me that the hon. gentleman has doubts whether in fact that will turn out to be the case. This underlines the concern many of us feel about Canada's future trading relations.
Overriding all these things is the need for the government to develop an adequate economic strategy to deal with our economic problems. This strategy must take account of the growth of multinational corporations, the influence of technology, the need for the rationalization of much of our industry and the attendant specialization that goes with it. Trading problems are, of course, closely related to all this. Thus I think it is essential to Canada's future and for the well being of our people that the government develop its policy more adequately than it has up to the present time.

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY ON SCIENTIFIC AND TECHNOLOGICAL CO-OPERATION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while listening to the preliminary report presented by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and seeing him table the agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany on Scientific and Technological Cooperation, we are happy to find that our relations with that country are better at the present time than they were thirty years ago.
I hope this agreement on scientific and technological cooperation will bring about advantages to both countries and mainly to Canada. However, this agreement should not be profitable to only one party as in some cases, where one puts in a horse and the other a rabbit. Agreements must be made on an equitable manner in order that the two parties may benefit from research made in either country. If expenses have been incurred to allow Canadian businessmen and industrialists to see the developments in Germany and compare their costs with those in Canada, I trust they were profitable, not only to those businessmen but also to the people who depend on them.
I am thinking, in particular, of the high rate of unemployment in Canada; we can compare it, for instance, to the rate in Germany, which the minister visited. Advice might also be sought, not only with regard to industry and business, but administration, to acquire experience. We won the war, it seems, but at first glance it would seem that we have lost the economic war to that highly industrialized country.
As we read the minister's report, as well as several others, it seems that the development of the European Common Market is of great concern to countries which do not take part in it, in particular to Commonwealth countries. It seems that as the mother country abandons its children, they find themselves helpless.
I note that, in his report, the minister says that he strongly encouraged Germany to step up its interest in Canadian agricultural products, which puzzles me. While Germany is invited to take an interest in Canadian
agricultural products, we feel free to buy some of these products which may be grown at home from other Commonwealth countries.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce told the members of a Senate Committee on November 4, 1970, that we had imported in 1969 for $60 million worth of beef and lamb, and that in the statements made at that time, the government, the department had even taken the lead.
Now it seems to me that there is a conflict between the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture. Trade consists in buying for re-sale. I see no other reason for those invitations to trade.
So instead of buying from other Commonwealth countries goods we can produce, let us invite Germany to deal direct with Australia and New Zealand, to obtain the farm products it requires.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope these efforts will be profitable for Canadian businessmen, for Canadian industry, and will contribute somewhat to solving Canada's unemployment problem.

subtopic: STE. SCHOLASTIQUE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
STE. SCHOLASTIQUE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I raise a matter of urgency which in my opinion must be put before the House.
For all practical purposes, the work at the Sainte-Scholastique airport has been stopped owing to jurisdictional misunderstanding between the federal and provincial governments. Both those governments are accusing each other of being responsible for that situation. If the manpower crisis continues, the project will be considerably delayed and the citizens will again pay the costs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask unanimous leave of the House to consider the following motion, which I move seconded by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell):
That the House direct the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications to study the problem ol manpower at Sainte-Scholastique, to report completely as soon as possible to the House on the state of the situation and to make recommendations likely to put the project back into operation.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister a question concerning the consultations that officials of the government propose to undertake with Washington regarding the proposed TAPS pipeline which, according to the Prime Minister's parliamentary secretary, are to include questions relating to pollution, including the volume of oil to be moved. My question is whether his officials intend to ascertain not only the volume of oil to be moved, which is quite well known, but the place to which the oil is to be moved.
I ask this question because of the importance of knowing how much oil is to be moved through the Strait of Juan de Fuca and in view of the indications that a pipeline may be built from there to the midwest involving the movement of as much as one million barrels a day, despite the statement of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that he knew nothing about the prospect of any such pipeline. subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, I have a few thoughts that I had expected to get on the record last evening but was unable to do so.
First of all, in discussing the question of the government of Canada laying down a labour standards code, one really has to analyse who will be affected by it. It will be, basically, the unorganized labour sector of our society and the small, private business sector of our society. Really, in laying down a system of labour standards one can outline the hours of work and conditions of work, but many of the decisions on these aspects are made, in relation to what one might call the larger corporations, through labour negotiations with the unions. In the small, private business sector, we do not have the same provision for negotiating hours of work and labour conditions. So, there is a need for the federal government to lay down labour standards. In fact, if the federal government creates undue hardship in the small, private business sector by making the labour standards code too strict or by enforcing too rigid a pattern, then the cost of doing business in that sector is increased. One must be careful, therefore, to balance the situation in the small, private business sector with the organized sector, because individuals in both groups must live in the same environment. The non-organized worker must live under the same living conditions.
If we allow a system to evolve in which organized labour is able to acquire rapid and continual increases in wages, then of course these wage increases will have an effect on inflation. They contribute to inflation in the economy and, once again, labour will be drastically hurt unless the minimum wage is increased. This bill, in fact, increases the minimum wage and creates a situation
Canada Labour (Standards) Code wherein the minimum wage can be increased automatically by the governor in council. Up until this time, the minimum wage increase has come about through Parliament passing a bill to this effect. In fact, 1 believe it is less than a year ago that the minimum wage was increased from $1.25 to $1.65, and this bill would boost it up to $1.75. One could take that as an admission that we have allowed the economy to inflate at a very rapid rate, and have had to increase the minimum wage so that once again the worker might at least be able to cope with the inflated economy.
If we are to bring about some equalization of opportunity, and of working conditions, I believe the government of the day must realize that perhaps the time has come when we cannot keep on pushing up the unorganized workers' wages. Perhaps some action should be taken on the other side of the pendulum so that some government body or labour court could bring about some relationship between the organized and unorganized parts of our society. I know this has been attempted. Mr. Young of the Prices and Incomes Commission seriously tried, by the art of persuasion, to convince unions and corporations that prices should not be increased and that demands for higher wages should not exceed the rate of 6 per cent. I think we have reached the point in our rationalization when we can readily agree that this attempt was a complete failure. I believe Mr. Young was bitterly disappointed that his policy had no effect whatsoever on trade unions and had only a marginal effect on corporations. Of course, the corporations will make up for this in the coming year.
So, while we pass labour standards legislation setting out working conditions and number of hours, as well as a minimum wage, in respect of the unorganized part of our society, this really is not enough. We must study the situation and begin to do something about the other side of the ledger, because if we allow wages to increase practically out of hand sooner or later this will be reflected in the price of goods. When we get out of step with societies in other countries we find it necessary, as Canadians, to buy more and more foreign made goods which automatically creates less and less of an opportunity for the working man in Canada. As an example of this, one has only to look at the influx of Japanese automobiles, particularly in western Canada. One might ask what the reason is for this. They are good automobiles. They are allowed in because the economy has moved ahead and the cost of production has increased at such a rapid rate that a vacuum has been created into which the Japanese manufacturer can move.
The same thing applies in respect of the textile industry. Earlier the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) brought in legislation which, in effect, provides some kind of a stop-gap measure to temporarily protect the textile industry. The difficulty is that if we do that in respect of every piece of manufactured goods, we will continually move toward a state of isolation and this would seem to me to be the wrong step to take. The world is growing smaller and we are having more and more pressure placed upon us to be free traders. There-

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code fore, we must be in step with the other facets of our society and of the trading world.
It is interesting to note the direction in which we are moving today in Canada. In respect of trade and manufactured goods, we find we are a nation composed of ten countries. I abhor the thought, but in actual fact this is what is taking place. In some areas we find goods being produced by employees who receive very low wages. Since these goods are produced in a low wage area, they are able to move effectively into highly industrialized areas where the wages are very high. Immediately, barriers are raised within our society. I am referring here to the production of broiler chickens, for example. This is a direct example of how the low wages in respect of broiler chicken production in the agricultural sector of Quebec is having a harmful effect on the broiler chicken industry in the province of Ontario. The market is being undercut.
We are being asked to pass a bill which would establish the minimum wage in the federal sector at $1.75. One must compare that with the minimum wage in other segments of our society. The minimum wage varies all the way from 85 cents an hour to $1.50 an hour in the ten provinces which compose this country. Newfoundland has the lowest wage at 85 cents an hour for women and $1.10 for men. Ontario has the highest at $1.50 per hour for men. Politicians sometimes become agitated about being popular politically, but cabinet ministers should always put their country first. We should try to stay in step with our country and keep the levels of our society in step with one another. At times, I feel the present government is doing everything it can to completely wreck the private sector of the economy. It would seem to be doing everything it can to convince the people now engaged in the private sector that the best thing for them to do would be to sell out and go to work for the government or some giant corporation. I really do not know what motivates the government in this regard, but this is how it appears. The government is making it more and more difficult for the private sector to survive in our society. They are making it easier for the giant corporations and the government to be the major employers in our society. What is the purpose of bringing in a standard which is far above the prevailing practice in many fields in which people are employed? The federal Labour Standards Act will not affect a great portion of the unorganized workers because most of them come under provincial jurisdiction. Provincial legislation does not set minimum wages nearly this high, nor are the conditions as stringent.
If the provinces felt that they could become popular by suddenly increasing minimum wages, I think they would. What would be the net affect? It would be an increase in the cost of production in those regions. In many of the regions where there is high unemployment, governments are trying to create opportunities rather than bring about a situation in which fewer and fewer opportunities will exist. I am certain even the Liberal government in Newfoundland would like to enact a higher minimum wage
level, but this would make it very difficult for the private sector in that province to survive. Therefore, they are reluctant to do so. Most provinces have to place the emphasis on the creation of opportunities, not on the security of those already employed.
At a time when approximately 600,000 people are unemployed and the government is prepared to spend $58 million to keep the youth occupied by this summer, we cannot say that we are happy and contented. We cannot pass legislation which will only serve to make a certain cabinet minister popular. We have to create opportunities, not protect the well established firms, businesses or enterprises and the working men who have secure jobs.
Many portions of this legislation are very good. The severence pay concept is good, but my belief is that it does not go far enough by only allowing two days severence pay for every year that a person is employed. If a person is employed for five years, he receives payment for 10 days when he is released, fired or laid off through no fault of his own. Although it does not go far enough, it is a step in the right direction.
The whole concept in the House of Commons today is to repeatedly pass legislation which narrows the opportunities for Canadians. I have to point that out with regard to every piece of legislation that comes before this House, because this is the only way I can get the message across to the people of Canada and this government. We have to broaden the opportunity for Canadians to participate fully in our society. This legislation does not do anything in that regard. It attempts to protect those people already employed and, at the same time, narrows the opportunities for those people who are unemployed. For that reason, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) should not find any great pleasure in having this legislation passed. He should perhaps do this dutifully, but in conjunction with labour legislation which creates opportunities for employment. We have not seen such legislation yet.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank three members for their courtesy in yielding their right to speak to me at this time because I have an engagement later this afternoon outside the city. They are the members for London East (Mr. Turner), Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg).
I wish to make three comments on the measure before us this afternoon. The first is with regard to the minimum wage. I know the difficulty of trying to establish one figure which will be suitable for all Canada. As I am not wiser than Solomon, there is very little I can say in that regard.
The idea of giving the Governor in Council the right to establish these wages in the future is fraught with danger. I suppose the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is aware of the danger. Perhaps I can put my fears on record so that they can be dealt with in committee. This approach may put the Governor in Council under a great deal of stress at certain times, probably once every four years. Also, it could be capable of abuse. At least the advantage of having the change made here is that we

April 27, 1971

have an opportunity to openly apply pressure to see what we can come up with. The minister should be specific in committee and spell out the factors which will enter into the formula for the minimum wage so that we, and through us the country, will have a good idea just how the wage is determined for the 530,000 people under federal jurisdiction. In this way, a lot of grief for the Governor in Council can be avoided in the future.
The second point on which I want to comment concerns the equal pay provision. I have no quarrel with that in principle. It is a step forward that the policing will not have to be done by the individual. In the past, a woman usually had to complain that she was being discriminated against. That is an awkward burden to put on any person. We are not all ready to yell for our rights, and perhaps more women are in this category. If a woman does yell for her rights and gets them, she fears that she may be shown the front door of the factory. It is much better to have the department do the policing. I suppose the department will still be following up complaints. As this part of the bill is remarkably brief, I suggest that some policy of warning to employers might be instituted so that they will not be hauled holus-bolus into court as a result, perhaps inadvertently, of breaching the law.
One question which may be interpreted one way by the employer and another way by the employee is whether a female employee is doing the same sort of work as the males in the plant are doing. That may be a contentious factor. The employer might, in good faith, have a different level of wages, but the court may consider that both the male and female employees are doing the same type of work and that the female is being discriminated against. There has to be an element of common sense in the policing and enforcement of this section of the act, particularly as the law is now compressed into these two subparagraphs.
I welcome the maternity leave provision. It is indicative of a measure of civilization and common sense. I do not think there will be any danger of abuse through the granting of such a right to the female portion of the work force. As I promised to be brief, I will simply say that I welcome this principle.
Finally, I wish to deal with the question of the extension of the 40 hour work week. When the act was originally introduced, there were some, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who felt there should be very little derogation from the 40 hour work week.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general objectives of the amendments to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code are to provide minimum standards and benefits not previously provided under the Code and to update some of the existing standards. At this time I wish to talk about two parts of the bill which I believe must be drawn to the attention of members of this House for their consideration: first, group termination of employment and, second, individual termination of employment.
The introduction of these changes will provide federal employees with the minimum protection from the less responsible employers. Looking at the railroad industry since the introduction of diesels, we find that drastic cuts in the work force have taken place and many who were once proud employees of the nation's railways now find themselves on welfare during the winter months. Due to the fact that they were over 40 or 50 years of age when the lay-offs took place, it was not possible for many of these employees to be reabsorbed into the labour market on a permanent basis.
Each year many industries in Canada make changes in their production methods; many decide to lock the door and move to some other part of the world. The rapid pace of technological progress and economic growth can and does have adverse effects on the working population. If resistance to change on the part of employees is to be less harmful, as must be the case if Canada is to achieve its full potential as an industrial power, trade unions and governments must accept responsibility for the develop-

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code ment and implementation of policies designed to cushion the impact of change on individuals.
More and more, Mr. Speaker, people of this nation are becoming aware that high labour costs have been leading managements in Canada and the United States to think in terms of closing out Canadian plants and transferring certain operations to other parts of the world. But the same managers seem to forget that the men they put out of work are also the consumers of their products. Most foreign demand for our products is concentrated, first and foremost, on our resource industries. Exports of grain, oil and gas, minerals and forest products are necessary to a trading nation such as Canada, but we must rely on heavy factory production and employment to provide the necessary lift to our Canadian economy. Any successful business is a combination of money and labour working toward a common goal of high production at lowest cost, so that both parties can compete in the home and export markets.
Down through the years employers and employees have worked hard to build many successful business establishments in this country, and much of their achievement has been accomplished with the help of foreign investment. We, as Canadians, welcome foreign capital but when the time comes for parent organizations to make any changes in the work pattern or plant operation, I say it must be done by prior consultation with the employees and their representatives. During the past few months, several plants in this country have closed down and it is certainly not in the best interests of the employees or residents of the communities affected to be saddled with the problem of relocating the employees without the help from the industry causing the shift.
For many years employers and trade unions have included in their collective agreements provisions designed to make the procedures governing lay-offs and recall more predictable and equitable, and settlements have included various arrangements to provide employees with some degree of protection against the effects of displacement. Governments, too, have recognized their responsibilities in this area and are pursuing policies designed to maintain conditions of general economic growth by offering a variety of manpower services, providing displaced employees with opportunities for retraining, relocation and job placement, providing short-term support for loss of income resulting from displacement under a general system of unemployment insurance and other special supplementary arrangements such as the transitional assistance benefit program which may apply when displacement results from government action designed to cause or accelerate industrial conversion.
Now, for the first time, the federal government requires appropriate notices of termination of employment to be given, thus enabling the manpower authorities to effectively utilize their various services. Bill C-228 provides that any employer who intends to terminate the employment of a substantial number of employees, and this includes managerial personnel and members of certain professions, shall be required to give advance notice to the Minister of Labour, the Department of Manpower
and Immigration and any trade union certified to represent the affected employees. The minimum period of notice required to be given varies with the number of employees involved. If 50 to 100 employees are to be dismissed, eight weeks' notice is required; if the number is between 101 and 300, 12 weeks' notice is to be given; if the number is greater than 300, 16 weeks' notice shall be given. Notification shall include the proposed date of termination and the estimated number of workers concerned. Regulations will prescribe circumstances in which a lay-off will not be deemed to be a termination of service. Employers and trade unions shall co-operate with the manpower services to assist workers under notice of dismissal to find alternative employment. The Governor-in-Council may make regulations that include exemption of employees employed on a seasonal or irregular basis, and provide for notification of group dismissal of less than 50 workers where industrial or regional conditions are of particular significance.
Waiver by the Minister of Labour of dismissal notification is provided for where it would harm the interests of employees, be unduly prejudicial to employers, or seriously hinder the operation of the industrial establishment concerned. Enforcement of the notice requirement will be the responsibility of the Department of Labour, as is the case with a wide range of other provisions. Any employer who violates this part of the law would be guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction by a fine of up to $10,000 or, on an indictable offence, by a fine of up to $100,000.
The information supplied by employers proposing substantial job terminations in a relatively short period will assist the manpower authorities to carry out their programs to help the affected employees in such matters as placement, retraining, relocation and others. There is no existing federal legislation on group termination of employment, and therefore this legislation is desirable. The legislation proposes that an individual who has worked continuously for an employer for three months or more is entitled to at least two weeks' written notice of termination of employment or, in lieu of such notice, pay at the regular rate for the regular hours. This provision does not apply in cases of dismissal or just cause.
A special provision is included to deal with situations where employees whose positions become redundant have "bumping rights" under the collective agreement. In such cases, the employer must give two weeks notice to such an employee and to the trade union, and must post a copy of the notice in a conspicuous place on his premises. If the employer fails to give the required notices, he must pay two weeks' wages in lieu of notice to the employee who is ultimately displaced as a result of the bumping process.
A layoff is regarded as a termination unless regulations prescribe otherwise. Wages and terms or conditions are not to be altered during the period of notice without the consent of the employee. Compliance with the notice provision in a particular case lapses if the employee continues in employment for two weeks beyond the

April 27, 1971

notice period, unless he consents in writing, and any subsequent notice to that individual must comply with the proposed legislation. Notice of individual termination will not apply to managers, supervisors and members of designated professions. Absences which do not interrupt continuity of employment and the meaning of "regular hours of work" are to be defined by regulation. "Successor rights" also apply to this section. There is at present no federal legislation regulating individual termination of employment.
Six provinces, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Ontario and Quebec, have legislation requiring an employer to give an employee a specified period of notice or, except in Manitoba, compensation in lieu of notice on termination of employment. The Quebec provisions are contained in the civil code, which is at present under revision. In Nova Scotia, Ontario and Saskatchewan, to be entitled to notice of termination of employment an employee must have been employed by the employer continuously for three months or more. In Manitoba notice is not required if employment is terminated during an employee's first two weeks in a job, unless the employer and employee have agreed in writing that the notice requirements of the act will apply. In Newfoundland notice is not required during the first month of a probationary period established by mutual agreement.
In closing, I would like to point out that during the war years thousands of Canadians joined our military services and went overseas to protect our freedom and way of life. They did not worry about leaving a steady job because the basic fibre of democracy was being threatened. They were willing to make sacrifices to protect these principles. When they returned thousands of veterans went directly to new jobs, and once they became established in the communities of this nation they naturally thought that they were set for life. The foreign industries of this nation have a responsibility to these Canadian employees to make sure that in the event of close-out everything possible in the way of retraining and severance pay is offered to these displaced employees.
Governments must have rules and regulations to make it impossible for foreign industry to close out without disclosing to the government departments the reason for their action. It is tragic when industry forces hundreds of people on to the labour market at an age when it is impossible for them to make the necessary changes without prior consultation. No one is resisting change, but all branches of society must be fully informed of industrial change so that ways and means can be found to cushion its impact on the lives of all Canadians and communities.
Many changes in this bill must be complemented by changes in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, whereby close-outs and changes in working conditions will be the subject of negotiations between companies and unions under government supervision. I know that the minister is very concerned about all the details of the changes as well as the problems of the
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
working people of this nation as we move ahead into the seventies.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief comments on Bill C-228. I think the main points have already been made by my colleagues who have spoken previously. All members of the House would rather see free, collective bargaining than the implementation of legislation to govern such negotiations. At the same time, I hope that the provisions of Bill C-228 will provide some spin-off and not a brush-off by some of the legislatures of this country. It appears that in many cases it does take the initiative of the federal government to bring about changes in provincial laws.
It seems strange that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) would bring in a bill at this time to provide for wage uniformity, since the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) not too long ago was substantiating the wage differential that existed between certain areas of the country. I have in mind the dockyard workers at Nanaimo and at Halifax, whose wage disparity was not eliminated. I am pleased to see that at least the Minister of Labour sees the need for bringing about uniformity throughout the country in this regard; I hope I am correct in that assumption.
The greatest problem with any bill is the enforcing and policing of the regulations that must go with it. A short while ago Canadian National Railways was fined because they violated the provisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. I have before me an article dated Saturday, May 31, 1969 which reports that:
The Canadian National Railways was fined $175 in Quebec Superior Court tor violating the Canada Labour (Standards) Code for failing to pay three of its employees time and one-half during national holidays.
We all recall the recent statements in the House of Commons with regard to CNR. I am pleased to say that once again the Minister of Labour stated he would not stand for any of this type of manoeuvring on the part of a Crown corporation like Canadian National. I refer to the attempt to pay provincial rates of pay when the uniform standards provisions of the act should have applied. I hope this matter has now been resolved to the satisfaction of all concerned.
A short while ago, specifically on December 4, 1968, it was being suggested that a new law would be introduced to regulate lay-offs. At that time, pressure was mounting in the cabinet to introduce legislation that would prevent companies from laying off employees with little or no prior warning to the employees or the government. Let me refer to an article dealing with this matter which puts it in this way:
Two federal cabinet ministers have publicly denounced major layoffs in recent days. They contend that management made no effort to help labour adjust to unemployment.
Labour Minister Mackasey said in the Commons last week "I think the time has come for the minister of labour to convince his colleagues that legislation emphasizing management's responsibility to its employees in the area of technological change is long overdue."

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
Then, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) also said in the Commons:
-that recent heavy lay-offs, which caught both labour and government by surprise, raised the question whether it might not be necessary "to oblige companies by law to provide advance notice".
I am sure the dissatisfaction of the government and the Minister of Labour in this regard has brought about some of the changes we see before us at this particular time.
The only suggestion I should like to make in respect of this legislation is that it would require employers to give advance notice of up to 16 weeks in the case of mass lay-offs, and severance pay to employees with at least five years' service. Advance notice is required only in the case of lay-offs of 50 or more employees, leaving an apparent loophole for employers to spread their lay-offs over a longer period. I hope when the committee studies this bill it will take this situation into consideration. I have in mind irresponsible companies which would deliberately use the provisions of this bill to lay-off fewer than 50 employees in order to avoid the obligations of the provisions of this bill. I understand there have been lay-offs recently of fewer than 50, and everyone knows that this practice will become progressively worse as time passes. I am sure this is an area all of us will consider in the committee when the time comes, in order to determine exactly what should be done as far as amendments are concerned.
There is no need to repeat some of the thoughts which have been expressed in this House. Most of us agree that this bill is very necessary, and with some amendments could be a model bill acceptable throughout this country, particularly to labour organizations and responsible companies.
It is interesting to note that there is some danger in the provision for equal pay for equal work. We should realize there are some 2.5 million women in the labour force and that more than 50 per cent of them are married. Some of the provisions in this bill will require a great deal of regulation and policing in order to ensure some type of uniformity. I am sure that the provision regarding the same or similar jobs requiring the same or similar skills, effort or responsibility, might bring about definitions by employers. I am sure we will all be responsible when we consider this fact. We all realize that all too often women are not brought into so-called decision-making positions. I am sure that a simple law requiring equal pay for equal work will be completely inadequate, because the work may be comparable or similar but different job classifications will be adopted allowing women to be hired for lower paid positions. I am sure it is not the intention of the Minister of Labour to bring about this type of situation.
It appears that these provisions must be accompanied by regulations which will require that all job classifications be open to women. This suggestion will be considered when the bill is before the committee for further discussion. At the present time there are no laws in respect of equal pay for equal work which require that
all positions be open to everyone, regardless of sex. The provisions of this bill, I suggest, will not make any noticeable change in the present situation. Let us look at the situation in the House of Commons where we have one female member. This makes one wonder whether we consider there is equal opportunity for both sexes in so far as election to this House is concerned. I believe the government is serious in bringing about an end to discrimination and that it will make funds available for the staff required to seek out the inequalities which exist at this time.
In respect of maternity leave, I believe we must be serious when looking at the situation which exists. The bill before us requires a woman to have 12 months' employment with one employer to qualify for 17 weeks' maternity leave. To say the least, this does not seem equitable. Since an employer is not required to provide leave with pay, but merely an unpaid leave of absence, it is difficult to understand the need for such a requirement at this time. This provision limits a woman's mobility in the work force and restricts the amount of leave to which she may be entitled, in relation to her biological function of childbearing. It also seems to me that this is a most crucial time to a woman in the work force, a time when she encounters added expenses. This provision would still allow an employer to fire a woman who becomes pregnant if she does not have 12 months of continuous employment before the need for maternity leave arises. I hope this aspect will be seriously considered by the standing committee.
The committee must also consider the provision for 11 weeks' leave prior to confinement and six weeks after. This is another point which will receive the consideration to which it is entitled by the committee.
Let me now refer to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code suspense account. On January 15 a return was tabled in this House to a question I had asked. My question was:
What payments have been made into the Labour (Standards) Code suspense account and what wages have been paid out of it to entitled employees for each year 1965 to 1970 inclusive?
The answer was that there was a continuous increase in money paid in and a smaller amount paid out. I suggest that there must be a better method for the determination by various departments, not necessarily the Department of Labour alone, of these people who have paid into this account and who are entitled to some repayment.
I asked also what policies and practices were carried out by the minister to locate the employees who were entitled to payment, once a payment was received into the Labour (Standards) Code suspense account. The answer at that time was that a program to have the Department of National Revenue locate and advise employees of their entitlement was presently under trial, using social insurance numbers. It appears to me that by using the social insurance numbers these employees could be contacted and advised that they might receive the money they had paid into this account.

April 27, 1971

We realize that the railroad industry does often have deferments. I realize that it is practically impossible to adopt any regulation or guideline for operation in respect of the transportation industry. We should have some regulation or an agreement as a result of collective bargaining between management and labour covering the hours put in by truckers and railway employees. It appears there should be a determined effort made, perhaps with a little prompting by the minister, to bring about some resolution in so far as the hours of work of employees of the transportation industry are concerned.
In closing, I should like to say I am extremely pleased to note that provision in the bill dealing with the garni-sheeing of wages. I know of too many occasions when employees have lost employment because their wages have been garnisheed. In the past, this has been sufficient reason for dismissal. I am exceedingly pleased that the minister and the government have decided to bring in a regulation prohibiting the dismissal of an employee for this reason. Far too often we find irresponsible employers will take advantage of such a situation to dismiss an employee. This has been the case in respect of the garnishment of wages. The minister is to be congratulated for this move. I will be pleased to see this bill sent to the committee. It is not my intention to hold it up at this time. I am anxious to see it discussed by the committee and amended as they might see fit.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will take me but a few minutes to say the nice things that I want to say about the minister; the other remarks I will have to make will take a little longer. This bill, in so far as it goes, is a good bill. I would not imagine there are too many people who think there is no longer much need for the minimum wage provision. There are surprising and tragic numbers of young people and others still employed receiving the minimum wage. I think that any t	allows the government to ensure a minimum
Jnd a minimum wage is all to the good. I think this bill brings us up to date in this respect.
Then, there is the question of maternity leave. I think this provision follows the thinking of the population today, x do not believe anyone would object to it, except perhaps the men, because the other clause dealing with equal rights does not give this privilege to men, but then very few men ever get pregnant.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: There will be changes.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, all sorts of changes are possible. I am glad to see this section of the bill dealing with maternity leave, as opposed to the inclusion of such a provision in the Unemployment Insurance Act where, as I already indicated, it does not belong. But even under this bill, there will be a difference. Of course, I take it that the maternity leave _ provisions in this bill will apply to women who are in the labour force and who will remain in the labour force. In other words, this part of the bill will apply to women who will continue working after they have had a child. There is a distinction between the
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
women who have to make a living, who have to remain in the labour force after pregnancy and the majority of women who do not come back to the labour force. The latter group will not apply for the leave permitted by this bill. But under the Unemployment Insurance Act, with which we dealt a few days ago, no distinction was made between these two group. For that reason, I am glad to see the inclusion of the provision in this bill but not in the other one.
So far as notice of lay-offs is concerned, I think that is a worthwhile provision. The minister has made himself familiar with the problems arising in cases of mass layoffs which come almost as a surprise. In most cases, notice could have been given. This bill makes such notice mandatory, and again I think that is a good provision.
Enough has been said about equality of wages. I believe Canadians accept this principle. I am glad also to see the provision with respect to garnishment, as the member who just sat down said. It is a little thing but it is evil because the debt collectors never bother collecting. They secure a garnishee order and immediately hound the employer until he gets so sick of it that the next fellow who gets a garnishee order against him will be laid off or fired. I should now like to see the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) do away with garnishment completely. It is an old fashioned practice which serves no purpose in this day and age.
When we have dealt with these items in the bill I wonder if we have really dealt with our labour problems. This is the labour code, and I would have liked to have seen the brackets taken away and the act entitled the Canada labour code, not the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The bill covers little things which do not solve the vast problems of labour today. The problem is that the population at large is beginning to look with suspicion at organized labour and organized labour is beginning to defend itself, but neither one nor the other has a labour code to follow. We have no labour policy. We have been going along, adding item by item. We have this bill and we have other minor bills, but to say that we cannot deal with the labour problem because they are within provincial jurisdiction is nonsense. I think that today the federal government must take the whole labour question in hand and deal with it.
We have inflation, and what happens? We immediately have to institute controls, or at least the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) thinks we have to do so, and then we have unemployment. Then, we have another round of inflation. The employer blames the employee, and the employee says "it is not my fault, you are making too much profit, Mr. Employer". Then, there is the question of what to do with our unions. No one has set down a policy, nor has this government done so. What will we do with the problems of labour? I think they must be recognized as problems which we have left alone for too long.
The hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner) spoke about lay-offs as a result of the implementation of new techniques. He said, justifiably so, that it is not equitable to have people laid off and thrown on the welfare rolls merely because a new machine has taken over. He must also recognize that in order to keep up with the produc-
COMMONS DEBATES________________April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code tion capacity of other countries we must introduce new techniques. I would suggest to him, and to this government as well as to labour, that deadheading is not the answer. Deadheading is a practice of that part of our existing labour institution by which, if you do not need firemen because you no longer have fires in the boilers of steam engines you employ one anyway. In fact, an employer is required to train apprentices to be hired when there is no longer any need for firemen. That does not make sense, even to the gentlemen opposite.

speechtext: I should have spoken after you.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
But then what is the answer? In Toronto, the three large department stores send a mat to the three newspapers, the same mat appearing in all. It is not necessary to set up all the type, and the ad is printed on the same date. For years people have been employed by the three newspapers, days after this advertisement has appeared and the newspapers have been thrown away, to line up the advertisements, print one copy, which is then thrown away. Even to the gentlemen opposite this does not make sense, and it should not make sense to this government. However, no solution to that problem seems to have been found.
So, we have all these labour problems, but no answers have been provided in this bill nor in any other bill, nor has this government a policy. We are faced with strikes more frequently than ever. Can anyone tell me how a strike, which throws people out of work and closes down the factory, will ever improve the current position of the employer or the employee? What really happens is that at the time of the strike workmen go home without pay. They dig into their savings and into the strike fund which the union has provided. When these funds are exhausted they finally receive an increase which never makes up the loss which they sustained. In the meantime, the employers have lost their reserves, and it just becomes a tactics game. Surely, one hundred years after the institution of this old fashioned scheme of things we should, as a government, put forward some ideas by which labour can get its fair share of new techniques and new production, by which the employer can use new techniques, and by which the nation can prosper and increase its productivity. For months before a strike, labour becomes antagonistic. For months after a strike is settled, labour usually has not settled the details and is still antagonistic, so the loss of production continues. I have been involved on both sides of this question and I know what can happen to production. This is an evil thing and we have not done anything about it.
Surely, in this day and age we can find some method of dealing with labour-management disputes without having work stoppages.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Tell us how.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
At one time I introduced a bill telling how, and I will repeat the details for the hon. gentleman. But the question is not one of labour-management disputes; it is one of labour-consumer disputes. Management does not worry too much. It merely adds on the cost of a strike

and the consumer pays. Under the terms of the bill that I introduced when a strike is declared, instead of work stoppage actually taking place, people would continue to work but the profits made by the corporation during the time that its workers were without a contract would be taxed 100 per cent. No one would suffer; the country would benefit, and the dispute would still be settled through negotiation. Such a provision is not made in this bill, and there are other things which are also not provided in it.
I am trying to inform you, Mr. Speaker, of something that is a fact today. There is no sense in closing our eyes and saying that everything in the labour-management field is fine. The fact is that this is not so. Surely, Mr. Speaker, you have known for a number of years that there is irritation in this field, and we do not seem to know what to do about it. But somebody has to come to some conclusion, and I suggest it is the government's responsibility to come up with a full labour policy, a full labour code, rather than the few words that are in this bill. This bill should have been four times as long and should have included many other matters.
One subject which seems to be taboo, and which is not covered in this bill, is the election of union officers. It has been said that anyone who stands up and opposes the slate of union officers usually nominated cannot lead a free life any more. It is true that some unions have secret ballots in the election of officers, but most do not. Surely, it is time we settled that question and said that from this time on the election of all officers of all associations and fraternities should take place by secret ballot. Why can't we include that in this bill?

speechtext: For corporations, too?

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Corporations, fraternities, churches, everyone.

speechtext: And the cabinet?

speechtext:
I am speaking of responsible positions. If you were talking about electing deputy ministers that would be fine, but I do not think it is important for cabinet members.
We must also soon recognize unions as legal entities. If they enter a contract they must observe the terms of that contract and be responsible for them. At present, we have a wishy-washy situation because the courts have said that unions are really fraternal associations, and are not a body corporate. That is nonsense.
I have already said that this bill should not require much debate. All of its provisions are acceptable to the public at large. The minister has earned a kudo for including some of the things, such as prohibition of dismissal for garnishment of wages, and the provision of maternity leave. I think we should get on with the bill as quickly as possible, but also as quickly as possible we should deal with the whole range of labour problems and the provision of a labour code setting government policy once and for all. We do not have much time in which to tackle that larger issue.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have studied with interest the measures proposed in Bill
April 27, 1971

C-228, an act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and, in general, I support what other speakers from my party have had to say in principle regarding the proposed legislation. I believe that all of us in this House have a moral obligation to ensure that for the many people whom this bill will affect there will exist humane and reasonable standards of employment, under conditions which represent as enlightened an approach as we can bring to this important subject.
Clause 5 of the bill deals with the requirement of a ministerial permit for an employer to work any group of employees in excess of the maximum hours prescribed by the legislation. I have some reservations about the practicality of this measure, although I quite agree with the principle. It seems to me that a number of situations must surely arise in which an employer has urgent and immediate need to extend the permitted maximum hours of work of some of his employees, and where the requirement that he obtain a permit in advance would be quite impossible and unduly onerous.
As a simple, practical illustration of this I am reminded of a situation of which I have personal knowledge. A local contractor was completing work on a new roof on a commercial establishment. It was imperative that the work be completed as quickly as possible because any serious rainstorm could have resulted in extensive damage to the interior of the building. The contractor has scheduled the work for completion at the end of a certain week. However, when Friday came he found that his schedule would have to be extended by at least another working day. His only real option was to work his employees on the Saturday, or to trust to luck that there would be no weather damage if he did not. He chose to leave the work unfinished over the week end and the weather held fine. It seems to me that under the terms of this bill it would have been difficult for him to get a permit in advance in order to complete the work on the Saturday. I appreciate that general contractors are not covered by this bill. Nevertheless, I am sure that similar situations could arise affecting employers who will be subjected to the requirements of a ministerial permit. All I am trying to say is that I hope when the bill is studied in committee some more flexible provision will be made regarding the matter of ministerial permits.
On the matter of overtime work, I wonder if there is not some wisdom in pressing for incorporation in this bill of a practice which has been followed by certain provincial departments in my province of Manitoba. For example, I know that payment for overtime work in the provincial department of highways, which is done mainly in the summer months, is banked and becomes payable on a regular weekly basis to tradesmen during the winter months when they are most likely to be unemployed. In fact, it would be impossible for that department in Manitoba to employ its work force throughout the whole year with any degree of efficiency. In this way tradesmen benefit from having a more continuous income throughout the year, without the necessity of relying upon unemployment insurance benefits to provide them with an income in slack periods. I think that this system makes a good deal of sense, both from the employee's viewpoint
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
and from that of the government, his employer, which otherwise must subsidize him through unemployment insurance payments to compensate for the irregular nature of his employment.
On the matter of minimum hourly wages, I support the principle involved in this concept. However, I wonder whether the legislation really solves as many problems as some of its supporters think it does. Certainly, in some of our smaller urban or rural communities a minimum hourly wage of $1.75 per hour, as this act proposes be the case on July 1, 1971, would be quite an adequate remuneration to enable one to enjoy reasonable minimum standards of living. Indeed, in some areas it might be in excess of this and if employers who come under this legislation constitute a significant number of the employers in the area, this provision could then have the effect of obliging the other employers to establish in their businesses or industries a minimum wage structure which could even work some hardship.
On the other hand, in a large urban centre, and for someone who may be married, I do not think $1.75 an hour would accomplish the desirable objectives of this section of the proposed act. If one has dependent children in addition to his wife, and he is employed in a large urban centre at the minimum hourly wage, it may very well be that he would be substantially better off on welfare. We assume that with our welfare we are giving the minimum standard necessary, compatible with a reasonable degree of sustenance. Indeed, even assuming such an individual were to work the maximum permitted hours of work under this act, namely 48, his gross weekly income would be $84. A married man could almost certainly exceed this amount through welfare payments. I think the foregoing illustrates that this very important section of the proposed act requires substantial further consideration to see if amendments cannot be proposed which will remedy, in a more effective manner than the present bill permits, the situations to which I have alluded.
I want to commend the minister, Mr. Speaker, for the provision in his proposed act which forbids an employer dismissing someone solely because a court order has been issued garnisheeing a portion of his wages. Many people, through circumstances quite honestly beyond their control, become the objects of a garnishment order, which in itself is a sufficient hardship, embarrassment and obstacle to their becoming financially solvent that I do not think employers should be permitted to add to such an individual's hardships by dismissing him solely for this reason when he most desperately needs employment. However, we recognize that people do have garnishments and that this adds to the employer's trouble.
As a related act to the Unemployment Insurance Act, this proposed bill provides for pregnancy leave of 17 weeks, consisting of 11 weeks before confinement and six weeks after delivery. This is one area where I think improvement could be made in the proportioning of leave. Pregnancy is a physiological phenomenon and is not considered an illness. The date of delivery is uncertain, even under the best regulated circumstances.

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code Indeed, it is probably safe to say that not more than 50 per cent of births fall into the category of a week or two on either side of the expected date. Then, add all the problems of deciding when a pregnant woman may deliver and you are left with a wide margin for error on either side.
In addition, to the difficulty of deciding when the expected event will occur, both for the medical praction-er and the woman, there is the question of how long a woman can work before her confinement. This depends on her job to a significant degree. If she is in a sedentary occupation, such as stenographer, she may well be able to work almost the full time; if she is in a more manual occupation she may be required, both for safety and production, to leave her job much sooner. After delivery, when complications may well arise, six weeks does not seem too much. In my observation, it is significant that most women do not return to their original employment. This may not be true in very large companies but it certainly bears investigation. Women often choose an occupation, usually at a lesser salary and with lesser work, in order to be able to devote more time to their family or to be closer to home.
I would like to see this section changed to 17 weeks to be given totally, proportioned as the woman herself decides. If she wishes to work up to nearly the time of her delivery and her employer is willing, it seems that she should be entitled to the full 17 weeks. I do not think it is practical to divide the time into two periods. This would create a lot of injustice and would not be happily received by many people.
These are a few short observations that I have on this bill, Mr. Speaker. I hope that in committee some of the provisions I have mentioned can be improved, and I will look forward to that.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
this bill is important because the few provisions which it proposes to add to the Labour (Standards) Code can and will have an effect on millions of Canadians. When we passed the original legislation in 1965, we set the minimum wage for workers under federal jurisdiction at $1.25 an hour. At that time I doubt if any province in Canada had a minimum wage for workers under provincial jurisdiction of more than or even up to $1 an hour. A recent survey indicates that in the province of Ontario the minimum wage under the Employment Standards Act is now $1.65; in Quebec it is $1.45; in British Columbia $1.50; in Newfoundland it is $1.25 for men and $1 for women; in Manitoba $1.50 an hour, and in Saskatchewan $1.15 an hour. I have no doubt, therefore, that if we increase the minimum wage from the $1.65 at which it was set some months ago to $1.75, this will have a very fast effect on provincial governments. We will see similar increases in the provinces and I support that completely.
When introducing the legislation the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) made the valid point that it is particularly important to the 60 per cent of the labour force which does not belong to trade unions, and do not have the protection of collective bargaining and union rates of pay. For those people who do not belong to
labour unions, the only protection with regard to wage rates is that given by legislation such as this or by the minimum wage legislation passed by the respective provinces.
A high percentage of unorganized labour has to depend on the protection provided by legislation. So, I am disturbed by the fact that in the year 1971 the minister has seen fit to propose a minimum wage as low as $1.75 an hour. That comes to just $3,600 a year for the person who works 40 hours a week, 50 weeks a year and gets two weeks off.
