speechtext: What did you say it was in Manitoba?

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: I said it was $1.50 an hour in Manitoba. I have already said, if the parliamentary secretary would take the trouble to listen, that the provinces traditionally follow the federal government. The parliamentary secretary, who I presume met with the ministers of labour of the provinces who were here last week, should know the province of Manitoba intends to raise its minimum wage again in the near future. The federal government has always set the example. I would hope it would set an example in this case. It is easy for the federal government to do this. Only a parliamentary secretary as stupid as this one would not know that-

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext: Keep it non-political.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
If the parliamentary secretary, who is not sitting in his own seat, would stop making stupid interjections I would ignore him, which is what he deserves. He should know that the industries which come under federal jurisdiction are by and large the railways, airlines, flour mills, the telecommunications systems and the banks. These can afford to pay the higher minimum wages proposed in the federal legislation. For this reason, I would expect any federal government, no matter what party is in office, would have a higher minimum wage than any provincial government, regardless of the party in power in that province.
I say the $1.75 proposed in this legislation is completely inadequate. The $3,600 a year, on the basis of $1.75 an hour a person would earn under the provisions of this legislation, is below the poverty line established by the Economic Council of Canada for a family. I suggest that the parliamentary secretary read-if he can read, which I sometimes doubt-a statement on income security which was made public this morning by the National Council of Welfare. This National Council of Welfare is not an NDP organization, an organization established by some trade union bureaucracy or an organization established by some revolutionary radical movement. It is an organization appointed by the federal government. It has, as members, representatives from every province in Canada. I would assume this government would have appointed to it people who are not very revolutionary. I would assume they would be people who, if not Liberals, would certainly not be very antagonistic to this government. I would commend to the members of the government, and the parliamentary secretary, this report because it deals with the whole question of income. I believe it gets to the guts

April 27, 1971

of the type of things I am talking about, the difficulty in respect of a minimum wage of $1.75 an hour in the year 1971.
For the benefit of the parliamentary secretary, I might read a few excerpts from this report. It points out that a large number of people do not have adequate income at the present time in Canada and that these can be divided into three groups. The first group is that of a family which has no employable member. The second group is one in which no employment is available for the employable member of the family. We know that almost three quarters of a million people are unemployed at the present time in this country. In the third group, the income from employment of the employed member or members of the family is inadequate to the needs of that family.
The report points out that it is estimated there are almost four million Canadians represented by families in which the earnings are less than the amount required to meet their needs. Need I remind hon. members of this House that there are people living on farms in Canada, people engaged in fishing, people living in the bush and Indian and Metis people whose income is far below the poverty level established by the Economic Council of Canada. I shall read one section of this report:
We have ensured that the stigma of poverty-
"We" means the people of Canada and the government.
-attaches to, the children of the poor by providing insufficient income for them to dress as their classmates, to afford a class picture as their classmates, to participate in class outings or extra-curricular activities involving expenditure. When they consequently learn to hate the school situation in which they are thus made to feel inadequate, drop out at the earliest opportunity in quest of a job-are the first to be laid off and thence drift into delinquency and crime, we blame the "culture of poverty" and talk piously of "cultural deprivation".
What amount is required to maintain a family? Let me quote what the National Council of Welfare says:
The Quebec Government Commission, updating Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures to 1971, identified these as $2,000 for a single person, $3,400 for a family of two adults, $3,900 for a family of three, and $4,560 for a family of four.
I believe I have already pointed out what is to be provided by this legislation. The fact is that the minimum wage in our country is to be something in the neighbourhood of $3,600. So, if this legislation is passed we will continue to ensure that a large number of people who come under federal jurisdiction because of their employment will be working fully but will not be earning enough money on which to live in anything but poverty. I do not think that is good enough. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), has a bill on the order paper which would set the minimum wage at $2 an hour. The Canadian Labour Congress suggested it should be set at $2.50 an hour and the Canadian Railway Labour Association suggests in its brief to the government that the minimum wage should be set at $2.25 an hour. I would be prepared to accept any of these suggestions but I am certainly convinced-

I do not think the government of Manitoba will follow any Liberal lead, and the parliamentary secretary knows this. I cannot accept the proposal of the minister that the $1.75 an hour in the future be amended through order in council as need is demonstrated. We have seen-and I shall deal with this later in respect of another aspect-how difficult it is to get the government to act. I had hoped the minister would have been prepared to spell out in this legislation that the $1.75 an hour he is proposing, which I have already said is much too low, would be adjusted annually and automatically based on increases in the cost of living.
With the exception of last year, we know the cost of living has been going up something in the neighbourhood of from 3 per cent to 5 per cent or more a year. This year's increase in the first three months of 1J per cent indicates we are to have in this year an increase in the cost of living of between 5 per cent and 6 per cent. That being the case, I am not prepared to leave the adjustment of the minimum wage to the whole cabinet. I would not mind if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) could do it on his own, because I have a good deal more confidence in him than in most other ministers of the government. I certainly am not prepared to leave the adjustment of the minimum wage to the whole cabinet through order in council, because we know from experience how slow a process that can be.
Before I leave the question of a minimum wage, I want to repeat what I said in 1965. I regret very much that this bill does not provide for a basic wage of even $1.75, as it does for all employees who come under federal jurisdiction, and give protection to the workers in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. These two territories are almost entirely dependent upon the federal government for their way of life. Because of their tremendous distance from the main centres of population in Canada and their very difficult terrain, these areas have the highest cost of living in Canada. These two areas have a very high, if not the highest, percentage of native people, Indians and Eskimos, in Canada. This is not the time to go into the terrible problems which we have foisted upon the descendants of the original inhabitants of this country. The incomes of the Indian and Eskimo people of this country, whether derived from work or other sources such as welfare or pension, are a disgrace.
Yesterday I spoke to a Canadian who spent five years working in backward, underdeveloped Africa. That person spent last week not in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon, but in The Pas, Manitoba. She told me she had never seen the kind of poverty, hopelessness and despair in backward, underdeveloped Africa which she witnessed among the Indian and Metis people in The Pas.

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
It would have been very easy for the government to include a clause in this legislation which would give the protection of this miserly $1.75 minimum wage to the workers in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon.
I want to deal with one other matter, the supposed provisions in the act passed in 1965 with regard to the hours of work. The then Minister of Labour hailed this act as a great step forward, since it provided for not only a minimum wage but a 40 hour week. When the bill was originally introduced, it provided that where industries might be adversely affected by the implementation of a 40 hour week, they could apply to the department for a deferment before the 40 hour week provision would be implemented. The act provided that the minister could give up to an 18 month deferment. At that time, some hon. members, including myself, protested that the 18 month deferment was too long a period of time. I must confess that I was an extremely naive Member of Parliament in 1965. I did not realize that not only could the minister give an 18 month deferment, but by taking the request under advisement he could in fact give what amounts to a permanent deferment.
Six years after being given such glowing hosannas about the paradise which this bill would create for the working people of Canada, almost every industry that comes under federal jurisdiction not only applied, but got and still has a deferment. The railway, marine, shipping and trucking industries still have not been brought under the provisions of the act with regard to the hours of work for workers.
The trade unions know the difficulties in their industries. At the time we passed the original bill, the Teamsters Union made representations to members of all parties about what might happen. The railway institutions made and are still making representations. The Canadian Railway Labour Association dealt with this problem in their April 19, 1971 submission. They agreed that there are problems which make it difficult to implement the sections of the act with regard to those who operate the trains. They made it clear in their submission that there is no excuse, six years after the original enactment of this bill for the non-operating employees, who represent 85 per cent or more of all railway employees, not yet being covered by the provisions of this act. If this is true, it denotes the most cynical collusion between the Department of Labour and the government on the one hand, and the railway employers on the other.
I hope the minister will make good the sentiments he expressed in his speech when he introduced this bill and that in the near future, certainly within a year, the number of workers who are still exempt from the protection which this bill supposedly gave to employees who come under federal jurisdiction will be reduced to the irreducible minimum. They would those employees for whom there is a relevant reason why the 40 hour provision cannot be applied.
I am going to vote for this bill, Mr. Speaker, mainly because what it provides can be agreed upon by all parties and all people in Canada. Those matters raised by the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) about strikes, the labour code and other matters can be debated in
more detail and more relevantly when the minister brings forward the amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which he has promised.

subsubtopic: PREVENTION OF MISUSE OF INFORMATION STORED IN DATA BANKS
speechtext:
that Bill C-38, to prevent the invasion of privacy resulting from the misuse of information stored in data banks, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be well for me to begin by outlining the reasons that I took it upon myself to bring forth a bill such as this one. It might seem to hon. members, and I am sure we will hear from them in the course of this debate, that a matter of this importance should be dealt with by the appropriate ministers of the Crown. After all, these ministers have the expertise of whole departments at their disposal. Surely, the country should not have to wait for a backbencher to bring forward a measure of this urgency and importance; a bill designed to meet the threat posed to the very foundation of our existence as a free people by the misuse of computer technology. Yet this is exactly what has happened.
The logical next question, then, is why is this independent action on my part necessary? Is nothing

April 27, 1971

being done by the Department of Communications? The short answer to that question appears to be that the departmental leadership is not especially interested in the role computers and data banks are playing in depriving us of a vital part of our freedom. Let me cite, for example, the words of the minister in a speech to the Montreal Chapter of the Data Processing Management Association on February 19 of last year:
It is not my intention here to dwell at length on the threats, real or imagined, that the computer utility poses for Canadians either individually or collectively. We are much more interested in the promise.
Well, I am interested in the promise, too; the promise of a future without Big Brother.
There have been a few glimmers of hope. In a one-sentence statement late last November it was finally announced that a special group within the task force on computer-communications will prepare a separate report on privacy. Even more significant perhaps is the fact that the Department of Communications did join with the Department of Justice, the Information Processing Society and Queen's University in sponsoring a conference on computers and privacy last May. To those assembled at the conference, however, the minister chose to deliver a speech some 14 pages in length during which he devoted only one and one-half paragraphs to the subject at hand, and those few words were spent minimizing the problem. "This conference", the minister said, "is a step, and no more than a step, in exploring the potential-and I emphasize the word "potential"-invasion and circumscription of privacy which may be brought about by the rapid development of computerized information systems and data banks." He closed his meagre remarks on the privacy issue by proclaiming: " I intend to say no more on the issue of computers and the invasion of privacy. In the first place I am in no sense an expert. In the second place, it is the business of this conference."
I am willing to admit, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans) may not be an expert, but I think the people of Canada have a right to expect that he at least approach this subject with the interest of a concerned layman.
Nor does the report of the telecommission issued earlier this month give much cause for satisfaction on this issue. Despite catchy headings such as "Soul in the System" and "The Human Goldfish" it is clear that the hand of the technocrat lies heavily on this report. This is only to be expected, for the primary concerns of the telecommission are technological issues. I submit, however, that privacy is very much a human issue and must be treated as such.
As I read the report, the authors argue that while there is a potential problem it is not one that we in Canada have to deal with immediately. Neither the public nor the private sector, they argue, are computerized to the extent we see in the United States and therefore it would be "premature to concentrate too much attention on locking the stable door before there is a horse inside." Well, Mr. Speaker, if we must sink to dealing in proverbs I have one for the Telecommission: "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure."
Data Privacy Act
So, as the Minister of Communications becomes more and more entangled in the Wired City where does that leave us? Well, fortunately, Mr. Speaker, there is a member of the cabinet who is concerned. I refer, of course, to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). He has stated on many occasions that he is alarmed about the growth of techniques which permit infringement on our privacy. Everything from devices the size of a pin which can transmit voices a distance of 25 miles, to parabolic microphones which can capture the conversations of persons miles away, to miniature cameras capable of photographing a subject two blocks away by moonlight-all of these devices can and are being used to destroy the privacy of Canadians. This is frightening, but there is a more severe threat yet. The minister expressed it in a speech last May. He said this:
The threat to privacy from electronic eavesdropping in both an individual and societal sense, pales before the privacy-shrinking enormities inherent in the computronics of data surveillance. It is here that the new information transfer technologies, with their capacity to accumulate, manipulate, store, retrieve, transmit and disclose information, come into their own.
The Minister of Justice then went on to quote Professor Arthur Miller of the University of Michigan Law School on the subject:
The computer, with its insatiable appetite for information, its image of infallibility, and its inability to forget anything that has been stored in it, may become the heart of surveillance system that will turn society into a transparent world in which our homes, our finances and our associations will be bared to a wide range of observers.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the time is close at hand. We must not delay taking corrective and preventive measures while we still can. In the August-Septem-ber, 1970, edition of Data Systems News, a trade journal of some considerable repute, Mr. Robert P. Henderson, Vice-President and General Manager of Honeywell Corporation's Electronic Data Processing Division, put it very bluntly. He said:
We have until, possibly, 1975 to come up with a solution. If we wait until 1977, it will already be 1984.
Mr. Henderson says "possibly 1975", 1975 at the outside. Do you really want to wait that long? Do you really want to live in a world where there is no refuge, where your every dealing, no matter how intimate, is known?
The Minister of Justice has said that he is concerned and alarmed. I believe that. I also believe that the Department of Justice is working on controls for computer systems. But the unfortunate fact is, as one of our leading newspapers pointed out not too long ago, the Minister of Justice has been concerned and alarmed since he took over the portfolio, and still parliament has taken no legislative action on this matter.
The reason for the introduction of my bill at this time, then, is to impress upon not only this government but upon governments at all levels that the time for action is now. What I am presenting is an alternative to the general lack of protective legislation for Canadians in this vital field. I have drafted the bill in the widest possible way so that hon. members may be able this afternoon to address themselves to almost any aspect of this most complex and far-reaching subject.

April 27, 1971
Data Privacy Act
Briefly, what Bill C-38 would do would be to establish a register of virtually all data banks in Canada. The operators of these data banks would be required to give the individuals concerned a print-out of all information stored about them, the names and addresses of all who receive it and a note on the purposes for which it has and is being used. There would be criminal penalties for failure to comply with the law and civil remedies for aggrieved persons. Individuals about whom information is contained in data banks would have the right to apply to have the information expunged or amended.
The bill does not, however, deal with another danger of the computer age-the storage of information about Canadians in foreign-controlled data banks. This omission does not mean that I think lightly of the danger of a situation in which, potentially, the nationals or government of another country could gain uncontrolled access to information about the private affairs of Canadians. Just the opposite. I believe this subject must be dealt with as soon as possible in legislation which would prohibit storage of such data outside our borders. Such legislation is a necessary companion-piece to the bill I am presenting today. The full title of this bill is "An act to prevent the invasion of privacy resulting from the misuse of information stored in data banks". In order to understand just what is meant by the phrase "invasion of privacy" we must examine the concept of privacy itself.
Is privacy really that important a factor in our lives? Must we have privacy in order to have dignity and freedom? The answer to these questions must, I submit, be an emphatic "Yes". To exist without privacy is to exist as something other than a full human being. Professor Charles Fried of Yale University has put it this way:
Privacy is not just one possible means among others to insure some other value, but it is necessarily related to ends and relations of the most fundamental sort: respect, love, friendship and trust. Privacy is not merely a good technique for furthering these fundamental relations; rather without privacy they are simply inconceivable. They require a context of privacy or the possibility of privacy for their existence. To make clear the necessity of privacy as a context for respect, love, friendship and trust is to bring out also why a threat to privacy seems to threaten our very integrity as persons. To respect, love, trust, feel affection for others and to regard ourselves as the objects of love, trust and affection is at the heart of our notion of ourselves as persons among persons, and privacy is the necessary atmosphere for these attitudes and actions, as oxygen is for combustion.
But does there exist a right to privacy? I would have to argue that in legal terms there is a very serious doubt that most Canadians can claim such a right. Canada has clearly been backward in this regard, especially in comparison to the United States. For example, the first article in an American legal journal setting forth the proposition of the right to privacy was written in 1890. The first article on this subject in Canada was not published until 1961, 71 years later. For over 70 years while writing, debate and legislative activity on this vital issue were taking place in the United States, Canadians did virtually nothing. This is a difficult fact to accept, but it
is true and it reflects badly on both our scholars and our
legislators.
So, it is that we must look to the U.S. experience. As I have said, the right to privacy was first seriously postulated in that country by Louis Brandeis and Samuel Warren in 1890. They described the right to privacy as the right to be left alone. Some 40 years after he had examined this right in the Harvard Law Review, Louis Brandeis, as Associate Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court, wrote a dissenting judgment that described in this way the philosophic underpinnings of the right to privacy:
The makers of the constitution undertook to secure conditions favourable to the pursuit of happiness. They recognized the significance of man's spiritual nature, of his feelings and of his intellect. They knew that only a part of the pain, pleasure and satisfaction of life are to be found in material things. They sought to protect people in their beliefs, their thoughts, their emotions and their sensations. They conferred as against the government, the right to be let alone-the most comprehensive of rights and the right most valued by civilized men.
So, gradually the majority of U.S. jurisdictions came to accept the right of privacy as a legal right providing protection for American citizens, while that right continued to have practically no status in Canada.
It was not until 1968 that the first breakthrough was made in Canada. In that year my home province of British Columbia passed its Privacy Act which Jerome Atrens, in an article in The Advocate, called "the first legislation of its kind in the Commonwealth". Mr. Atrens, a member of the faculty of law at the University of British Columbia, commented:
The enactment of the British Columbia Privacy Act is one of the most significant recent developments in the law of torts. Anglo-Canadian common law has never recognized an independent right of privacy. Under our common law the privacy of the individual receives indirect but inadequate protection through various causes of action, such as defamation, breach of contract, interference with a property right, trespass, nuisance and infringement of copyright.
The Privacy Act is the first legislation of its kind in the Commonwealth.
In the two and a half years since that article was written, the provinces have done little to advance the cause of protection of privacy; the federal government, nothing at all. The intention of my bill is to correct that act of omission in an extremely sensitive area, that of the improper use of computer technology.
The computer has quickly become a dominant influence in the commerce, industry and administration of western society. Experts rightly caution that the output of such machines depends on the material and facts fed into them. Men, not machines, are to be blamed for the abuses that may flow from "electronic brains". Electricity, gunpowder and the internal combustion engine are all valuable servants but dangerous when misused.
It cannot be denied, however, that it is the very efficiency of these machines that makes abuse both relatively easy and extremely tempting. Discussing the growing power of computers, M. S. Stone and Malcolm Warner, in an article in the Political Quarterly, note that the computers of 1968 were 1,000 times as fast as the largest of those manufactured in 1954. They have become smaller

April 27, 1971

and more compact while the cost of computing power and data storage has declined sharply.
In economic terms, it has become not only possible but profitable to maintain exceedingly detailed information on whole populations. In fact, the computer technology of today almost invites this. For example, if a corporation, or a government agency for that matter, is devising a form to be completed by its clients for later conversion into computer language, what is the difference if a few extra questions are added? They may not be relevant today but the answers might be handy to have a month or a decade from now. Before the advent of the computer such an attitude would have meant more work, bulkier files, and more difficult retrieval. Unfortunately for our privacy, this is no longer a problem.
Consider this case. In Washington, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration has awarded Honeywell a contract to develop a laser-storage technique that will allow one 4,500 foot magnetic tape to record and instantaneously feed back the equivalent of 12 pages apiece about every person in the entire United States. Less than one mile of tape containing the life history and habits of over 200 million people!
I must emphasize again that I do not mean to imply that computer technology is somehow bad and that data banks are dangerous in and of themselves. Of course, this is not the case. It is not some evil mastermind that I fear but rather those who, in the name of efficiency, start us on the road to that glass prison that is an existence without privacy. It happens that government itself is very prone to this sort of thing. Attacked on all sides for not being efficient, governments are apt to do what is expedient in the personal information field, much to the detriment of the people. An example of this type of thing, I believe, is to be seen in the decision of the government of Ontario to provide the following service, as reported in the Globe and Mail of December 15, 1970:
Anyone with $2 will be able to find out all your major debts in Ontario under a new computer storage system being launched January 1.
The searcher will have to get an account number with the Ontario Department of Justice, but anyone will be able to get such a number.
I am sure that this new system is much more efficient than the old method of searching through records in 48 offices across the province. Whether efficiency alone should be the criterion used to judge a plan such as this, I leave to the consideration of the people of Ontario. What would really bother me if I were a citizen of this province would be the decision the provincial government has taken to use the same data bank to store this information with information from another department. With just a slight change in the computer program, this could provide the basis for computer dossiers for most adults in Ontario. Legally there is no protection against such an abuse.
A potentially even more dangerous trend came to my attention last summer. On July 10, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) announced
Data Privacy Act
that the federal government was going to contribute over $97,000 toward a pilot project in Prince Edward Island to evaluate the use of social insurance numbers in providing health services to the public. According to the press release the project would "test the use of social insurance numbers assigned to P.E.I. residents in administering health services, in research and possibly in other social fields." I just wonder what those "other social fields" might be. I do not know. I do know that the use of social insurance numbers is being required more and more often on everything from tax forms to medicare applications. However, I feel I must sound a warning note. If the trend continues for individual Canadians to be known more and more as one specific set of digits, our social insurance number, then we may well be in very serious danger of loss of privacy. Because of the increasing compatability of the latest computers and their ability to communicate with each other, our social insurance number could become the key which would open up our lives to the unscrupulous data bank manipulator. Computer languages have become so standardized that data may flow easily in and out of separate systems. For instance, information about 705-113-405 could easily be traded between various data banks to form a complete record of the subject's dealings and activities. We must take steps to ensure that this does not happen.
In summary, put in its simplest terms, the problem is that many generations after the development of the original computer data systems, we still do not even have laws to govern the use of first generation computers. My bill will not solve all the problems I have raised this afternoon. I do not claim that. But it would be a start, and that is what is needed. The rapid expansion of the information processing art has left us with little time remaining to deal intelligently with the situation. We just cannot afford to put this vital matter off until next year,

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to commend the hon. member for bringing forward this bill. His last few remarks regarding this existing problem in Canada were very cogent. The time to move is now, because we do need some kind of control over the rapid explosion of the data bank systems in credit bureaus and other areas which is taking place in this country of ours. The privacy of individuals can be invaded very easily in this highly technological era in which we live.
I am amazed to some extent that a bill such as this should be brought forward by a private member rather than by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). We, in Canada, are sometimes motivated in our legislative thinking by fears which date back to the depression years of the 1930's. We are trying to pass legislation geared for the 1970's based on our thinking of the past. Certain legislation in respect of whether my wife or another housewife buys the proper size can of pork and beans must be based on eighteenth century thinking. Our whole education system has failed completely if we are no longer able to judge the per ounce cost of a can of beans which contains 28 ounces. I suggest this whole concept is misguided and motivated by fears which arose during the depression years. Perhaps this is understandable when one thinks of the sociological effects of a depression. Many people in the government and in the House of Commons today were of young and tender years during the past depression. This may have had a formative effect on our thinking.
Our computers are here to stay and we are wondering whether we can effectively manage machines or whether machines will manage men. This is a question of the 1970's and we are very concerned about it. About a year or two ago, I attended a seminar of UNESCO which studied the whole question of computers and data banks. This was attended by two members from each of the many influential nations which belong to the United Nations. They discussed what was being done in their countries. There were two members from Russia, two from Sweden as well as representatives from other countries. I was particularly interested in this subject matter as a firm believer in the suggestion that the individuality of man must be protected. Man must always have control over machines and the society in which he lives.
The rapid increase in the use of computer systems and data bank information is beginning to have more and more effect on our society. The Swedish delegates to this seminar explained that the government of Sweden has a national data bank system with information on everybody. If my memory serves me correctly, it is against the law there for anybody else to have such a data bank system. The government system contains all the factual information that can be gathered in respect of the individual. An individual can have access to that information merely by dialing a telephone number. One of the delegates suggested that this was perfectly all right. If an individual wanted to hire someone in Sweden, all he had to do was phone this number to find out the job that individual now held, how much he was receiving and how many jobs he had held over the last ten years. In other words, he could ascertain quickly whether an individual was likely to stay in his employ for some time. He could ascertain quickly what the individual's former employer thought he was worth by finding out his present wage. This seems to be a bit frightening.
The Swedish delegates went on to explain that this system went a little further. The government had developed a scheme whereby they could put an isotope on the fingertip of every person in Sweden. Instead of having a social security number, as suggested by the former speaker, each person would have this isotope on his finger. In this way one could gain access to the whereabouts of that individual at any given time. The isotope could be fed into a computer system and at any time within the range of the computer system a government official could find out in what part of the city that isotope was. He could even determine whether you were at home with your wife or in a neighbouring city, where you were supposed to be, or down the road and across the street.
It is a frightening experience to listen to educated men explaining how carefully and closely you could be watched by a machine. We in this country have reached the stage of having a social security number. But they were even thinking of putting everybody on a particular isotope which could be implanted in the finger tip and all you would have to do is record the individual so that a computer could indicate where he was at any given time.
Surely we have advanced far enough in the system of data banks, credit bureaux and the relationship that a credit bureau will have to a particular individual to sit down as educated people and say that we must bring in legislation to protect the individual against possible false compilation of information. A section of Bill C-38 deals very fully with the ability of an individual to dial and receive information about himself filed in the bank and to request that the information be changed. I would go further than is suggested in the bill. If the data centre is not prepared to change the information, it should be possible to sue them and take them to court because they are releasing false data about a person. Then at least the courts could decide whether they were releasing false data.
It seems to me that our whole society depends on the individual and on his having as much freedom as possible to do what he wants to do. Our society is geared to the belief that we must have a higher quality of life. In my way of thinking we cannot have a high quality of life if some persons are allowed to compile false data about us and to release it without our knowledge.
We have had extensive discussion in the House about the RCMP compiling dossiers on Members of Parliament and anyone else. We may have some sense of security because surely the information they compile will only be released to a few people. However, credit bureaux and data information banks release information for a price- information which may be completely false.
Another interesting aspect of data banks and credit bureau systems established in this country is that in most

April 27, 1971

cases they are owned by U.S. concerns: all the information is being fed to a computer in a foreign country. It seems to me it is high time we took steps to control this machinery. They could exchange data bank information for a price and data banks could be drained dry in exchanging information. This is a very alarming possibility, because an individual might now know what information is compiled about him by data banks and with whom they have exchanged it.
This bill attempts to set out rules and regulations whereby a data bank would have to inform the individual who has asked what information was given about him. He could then ascertain how it was used and whether it was used in a manner which might detrimentally affect the health and welfare of his family and himself. I believe it is very important that an individual in our society knows what information is being spread about him throughout the country and how it is being used. If we believe in the concept that the individual is the all-important being in our society, surely we must take concrete action to assure individuals that in fact the government believes them to be all-important. If we do not accept that concept we can no longer believe that we are striving for a higher quality of life for the individual, because the misuse of information compiled without the knowledge of the individual can be detrimental to society as a whole.
I commend the Ontario government for establishing some sort of control. I think that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, as I said at the beginning of my speech, is operating from a fear complex, which perhaps originated in the 1930s, that if in fact 20 per cent of the tax dollar is spent on education, a person in our society will sooner or later be sufficiently educated to understand what is the proper size of a container in which he buys his food. But even with the best education that our society can provide, we cannot match the complex data systems that are being established on the North American continent-and I stress the words "North American continent". We are alarmed, as individuals, at their wide use and at the misuse of information which may detrimentally affect our society. If the government will not bring in legislation to give the individual tools with which to cope with the complex situation in which he finds himself in the twentieth century, then it is failing miserably to live up to its responsibilities in this day and age.
I commend the hon. member for introducing this bill. I hope he will be able to convince the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) that action along this line should be taken. I hope the bill will be sent to committee where it will receive exhaustive study. I am not naive enough to think that the government will accept the bill as drafted, but I would like to think that after studying it the government will bring in a similar bill or one with the same purpose, that is, the protection of the individual from a computer system which can compile and release false information about him which might be detrimental to him and his family.

Mr. Speaker, briefly what is at stake here in our national policy with regard to computers. I suggest we have very basic objectives. We want to create in Canada a computer technology ol lull range Irom basic computers ol the so-called hardware type and design to the application ol special machines to serve business and consumers and to the creation ol computers to assist small, competitive businesses engaged in service to the public.
We want to create a leading place lor Canada in this industry because we recognize its basic importance in the development ol technology and improvement ol productivity in industry. I think we also want to provide a maximum range ol service to consumers. We want to prevent Iraud, and we want to make it possible lor consumers to use a credit card to purchase gasoline il they go on a trip to our neighbour to the south, rent a hotel room or purchase a number ol other things.
In an attempt to reach these basic objectives I suggest we are obliged to distinguish between private and public use ol data banks and computers. The hon. member exempted Irom his bill certain categories ol police investigation and data banks used lor that purpose and other public services. However, I note that many areas in which the hon. member claimed there was the possibility ol abuse did involve government. He talked about possible extension ol social security numbers and ol a test project ol the Department ol National Health and Welfare to ascertain what can be done with the application ol these numbers. He raised questions about the possible extension to other areas.
The very areas he has excluded Irom the bill, government services, are those wherein the problem he posed arises in its sharpest form. On the other hand, there are developments in the area ol private industry, to which this bill would primarily apply, which I think would create unnecessary restrictions and impede the development ol a national policy with regard to the best use ol computers.
Along with a number ol other members ol this House I accepted the invitation ol a local computer firm last week when Systems Dimensions Limited asked us to visit them, see what they are doing and learn something about the computer industry. I very much appreciated their hospitality. The service they placed at our disposal, the senior staff now accompanied us and the opportunity to

April 27, 1971

freely ask questions gave us a better understanding of what goes on.
One thing that struck me forcibly was the elaborate provision for privacy which was the essence of their service. They operate 24 hours a day. In many businesses, after closing at five o'clock an hour or two is spent putting basic data on computer tape, which is then fed by electronic devices, or in some cases over the telephone, to the computer bank. However, this firm had an elaborate precaution, extending to every member of its staff, which ensured that information coming from one customer was completely shrouded in secrecy. They were selling the service to industry and prided themselves on the fact that they had built security and privacy into their data bank that was foolproof against raids by competitors. It was the essence of their service that the 150 people using it were confident that when they bought the service none of the information would be available to anyone else.
I was pleasantly surprised to find that this company had developed an export business fully competitive in its pricing and range of service. It has a number of customers south of the border who find that they can come to Ottawa and buy the service more economically and efficiently than in neighbouring northern United States cities.
The hon. member who proposed this bill would prohibit the use of memory banks across international borders. I suggest that this cannot be prohibited. It has to be examined on its merits. We are developing an industry in this country with a population of 21J million people and the very essence of the industry is that it should be free to compete for business in the large market to the south. If we are prepared to do business to the south, we must be prepared to allow businesses based in the United States to have certain reciprocal access to our market where we offer a specialized service.
I use an international brand of gasoline and I cannot conceive of the situation where I cannot use my credit card almost anywhere on the North American continent. I know very well that when I make a purchase on my credit card, the details of the purchase will go into a computer bank. I would be naive to think that the computer bank would have to be located in Canada through any type of legislative compulsion that would fly in the face of the economics of the industry. I want to the service of that credit card and I have to face the consequences of the industry having a certain international aspect.
I agree with the intent of the bill, Mr. Speaker, and I agree that this is an important question. It deserves a place in the legislation not only of this House but of all democratic societies in the western world. The answers are not simple; they are not black and white-but they do not involve a prohibition on computer information going across an international border. They do not, I think, involve placing elaborate, red tape restrictions on access to information from data banks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues have dealt very thoroughly with our criticism of a number of the features of this legislation and it is my intention to emphasize only two of the points in the bill, the provision that deals with equal pay for women and the provision having to do with maternity leave.
This bill provides for the repeal of the Female Employees Equal Pay Act of 1956 and its replacement by new provisions. The minister emphatically explained that these new provisions are stronger than those in the old legislation. We certainly hope so. Under the old act differences in rates of pay were prohibited for men and women performing "identical or substantially identical work". Under the proposed section of the code this prohibition is extended by referring to "the same or similar work on jobs requiring the same or similar skill, effort and responsibility". The wording undoubtedly is more elaborate and detailed. I wish the minister had been a little more detailed in his explanation of the difference. I hope there is a difference and not merely a change of wording. I hope, also, that this provision will really represent a difference in practice. One wonders how fool proof the new legislation will be in practice.
The president of the Canada Labour Congress has referred to the fact that this provision is somewhat loosely worded: it is not very explicit. The new provision will make evasion a little more difficult for employers. It will still allow them to pay women at a lower rate for work which involves more skill and responsibility than work done by highly paid male workers. This situation exists in some industries. The minister said he wanted to carry

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
out the recommendations in the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. Paragraph 218 at page 67 of that report reads:
Canada has not, however, ratified the International Labour Organization convention concerning equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value (Convention 100). We believe that Canada should do this. Therefore, we recommend that a federal-provincial conference on labour legislation affecting women in Canada be called to prepare for Canada's ratification of the International Labour Organization convention concerning equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value (Convention 100).
The minister could indicate his stand with regard to this point which is made in the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. I would like the minister to specifically state whether at the recent meeting in Ottawa the labour ministers discussed this point. Could I get the ear of the parliamentary secretary for one moment? I would like the parliamentary secretary to take note of this question. When the minister replies, will he state whether during the labour minister's conference there was discussion on the advisability of Canada ratifying the International Labour Organization's Convention 100. This is a recommendation of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women.
The Canada Labour (Standards) Code affects approximately 530,000 employees who are under the jurisdiction of the federal Department of Labour. There are approximately 2.5 million women in the labour force. In order to have effective legislation regarding equal pay for equal work, it would have to be parallelled by provincial legislation. Will the parliamentary secretary inform the minister that we would like him to report on whether this matter was also discussed at the recent labour ministers' conference and, if so, what was the result? If there were discussions, what was the general feeling about the possibility of getting parallel legislation in the provinces which would make the equal pay changes effective in the provinces?
One big improvement in this legislation, to which the minister referred, is the matter of complaints. He stated, quite rightly, that under the old legislation women were afraid to complain because of the fear of still further discrimination. Under the new bill, the minister stated that the onus will be on the inspectors of the Department of Labour to lay complaints and launch prosecutions. These provisions are only as good as the system of inspection that is established. How thorough will the inspection services be, and how will they be enforced? The fines will be higher, but not much higher than those under the Combines Investigation Act which have been criticized as being very inadequate for large firms.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), suggested that the Department of Labour should do more than just wait for complaints to turn up. He suggested that where more than 80 per cent of the positions in any job classification are held by members of one sex, the minister should order an investigation into the hiring, training and promotion practices of the industry concerned to see whether there could be a more equitable balance as between male and female employees. We do not say this should be on a 50-50 basis,
but where there is a large discrepancy between the number of male and female workers there should be an investigation into the hiring, training and promotion practices. A number of these points should be considered in committee.
While the new legislation is an improvement, it will be no better than the inspection and enforcement of its provisions. It will not be widespread or universal unless the provinces follow it through. I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) will not wait for the provinces to do this on their own. One of the jobs of a federal minister ought to be to persuade the provinces and to follow through good legislation if only for the reason that there is a great deal of mobility of workers across Canada. There is no use having protection for a worker in one province if he moves to another province which is not under the legislative umbrella. This is equally true of women workers.
I want to deal briefly with the maternity leave provisions. I wish to express my satisfaction that the m.nister has introduced these two companion provisions. They represent a real advance in the promotion of women workers in Canada. However, I must make some criticism because this legislation does not go far enough. Although it is a step in the right direction, it is far from perfect. Many people will now be experiencing a degree of protection which they did not have before.
One shortcoming in this legislation is that an employee must be employed for 12 months with the same employer in order to qualify for 17 weeks of maternity leave. As the employer will not be required to provide leave with pay but merely unpaid leave of absence, it is hard to understand the need for such a requirement. We would like to know wherein the need lies. It limits a woman's mobility in the work force and restricts the recognition of her right to be in the work force regardless of her biological function of childbearing. At a time when a woman is most in need of a job because of the additional expenses involved, this provision will still allow employers to fire a woman who becomes pregnant if she has not had the luck to work for him for 12 months before becoming pregnant. This seems to us to constitute a real hardship and a shortcoming in the legislation, which ought to be modified. Here again, the minister has probably noted that his legislation differs from the report of the royal commission which recommended 18 weeks of maternity leave, not 17. Again, we should like to know the reason for failure to follow the commission's recommendation.
Moreover, the act only prohibits an employer from dismissing a woman solely because of her pregnancy. The royal commission suggested a blanket prohibition against dismissing a woman, on any ground, during her pregnancy. This blanket provision was recommended because it would prevent an employer from citing a spurious reason for releasing a woman when the actual reason for dismissal was her pregnancy. This is a situation in which the advice of the commission might well be taken. Many employers do not like having pregnant women in the labour force: as a matter of fact, they do not like having

April 27, 1971

women in the labour force at all and they might well be inclined to cloak their dismissal of a pregnant woman by some other excuse. For this reason it might be well to follow the commission's recommendation by flatly preventing dismissing a woman during her pregnancy.
Another criticism I should like to make concerns the lack of flexibility of the legislation. The clause providing for 11 weeks' leave prior to confinement and six weeks after should be changed so as to eliminate the distinction between before and after childbirth. There is little reason for most women to sit at home and do nothing in the last 11 weeks prior to childbirth. I beg your pardon, Mr. Speaker; I am afraid my sore throat is the result of our convention.

I should like to make a few observations at this point before the bill is referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. First, I hope the measure will be passed expeditiously in order that these amendments may take effect on the proposed date of July 1 this year.
As we all know, federal labour standards were first introduced in 1965. The importance of these standards rests on the example the federal government sets for

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
other jurisdictions as much as on the degree of assistance given to the limited number of employees presently working under federal jurisdiction.
In 1965, the first federal code established the minimum wage at $1.25 an hour. In July, 1970, this was changed to $1.65, and in these proposals it is suggested this figure be amended to $1.75. I support this proposed change, but more importantly I endorse the fact that under this legislation the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, can increase the figure from time to time without specific legislation being required. The power given to the minister and to the Governor in Council will, I hope, eliminate the long delays in making changes and, hopefully, will result in an annual review of the minimum wage for people working within federal jurisdiction. I hope the committee will give consideration to recommending that the Minister of Labour review this minimum standards annually.
This bill is of particular importance since we have an obligation to protect the unorganized labour forces in Canada which come within federal jurisdiction. Hopefully, as I said before, this legislation should set an example to other jurisdictions and encourage them to take the same action within their areas of responsibility. Most of the members of this House realize that approximately 60 per cent of the labour force of Canada is without the protection of a labour union. On the federal level there is a 50-50 split between organized and unorganized labour. In view of the large numbers of people concerned, these amendments assume particular importance.
The minimum wage standards set in this legislation do not apply to employees under 17 years of age. In 1965 specific regulations were established to set the rate for such people at $1 per hour. In July last year, this rate was raised to $1.40 per hour. It is my understanding that the minister will recommend to cabinet, following passage of this bill, that the regulation be changed to establish the rate at $1.50 per hour. I hope that the minister will review the minimum wage for those under 17 years of age in our work force at the same time as he reviews the over-all minimum wage for those over the age of 17, and that this will be done annually in both instances.
In clause 17, at page 13 of the bill, there is a provision dealing with the individual termination of employment whereby two weeks' notice, or pay in lieu of notice, must be given to an employee with three months' service or more. This provision will apply to all regular employees but not to those performing managerial functions or in professional categories. Frankly, I fail to see why this distinction must be made between ordinary employees and management or professional employees and I trust that the standing committee will look carefully at this question and satisfy itself that there are compelling reasons for making this exception. If there are not compelling reasons, I hope the committee will recommend the elimination of this distinction.
Still on clause 17, I want to talk for a few moments about severance pay and to support the provision where-

by an employee with five or more years' service receives two days per year severance pay, to a maximum of 40 days. Obviously, this does not apply to an employee whose employment has been terminated for just cause, or who is entitled to pension whether it be the Canada pension or the like. I hope the committee will give consideration to reviewing these provisions with the thought of establishing a two-day benefit for every year of service without the five-year minimum requirement.
I make this suggestion because it seems to me that if it is valid to give a person 10 days' severance pay after five years' service, then it is unfair to cut any benefit for a person with only four years and 11 months' service. If we were to establish benefits on the basis of two days for every one year of service, then after one year a person would receive two days' pay; after four years he would receive eight days' pay, and so on. I think that is a reasonable suggestion to make. Although the minister may well have some valid reason why it cannot be implemented, I hope the committee will carefully review this suggestion. Excluded from the severance pay provisions are those in a managerial or professional category. Once more, I fail to see why the distinction has to be made between them and ordinary employees.
The bill also covers group termination of employment. This proposed new part provides that an employer contemplating the termination of employment of 50 or more workers within a four-week period must give the Minister of Labour notice in writing. A copy of the notice must be sent to the nearest Canada Manpower centre and to the trade unions concerned. This part will apply to all employees, including persons performing managerial functions and professional people, but will exclude those who are seasonally or irregularly employed. I suggest that the committee give careful consideration to this proposal, because those employees who are not covered by labour union contracts-in other words, those who have an individual relationship with their employer-are not really given specific notice under this legislation.
I should like to read the provision on page 11 of the bill. The section deals with the notice that must be given to the Minister of Labour and to the labour union. As far as the person not covered by labour union agreement is concerned, the bill provides:
-and where any employee in such group is not represented by a trade union, a copy of such notice shall he given to him or posted forthwith by the employer in a conspicuous place-
I suggest that when the committee reviews the bill, it should give consideration to deleting the word "or" and substituting therefor the word "and", so that the bill would then provide that there is an obligation on the employer to give notice to the individual not covered by labour contract as well as to post that notice in a conspicuous place. I do not think that this proposal would be difficult to implement. Generally speaking, I am 100 per cent in favour of the provisions dealing with group termination of employment. I think they are long overdue. Under these provisions, an employer who wants to lay off between 50 and 100 workers within a four-week period would have to give eight weeks' notice; if he wanted to lay off between 100 and 300 workers he would have to
April 27, 1971

give 12 weeks' notice; and to lay off more than 300 workers would require 16 weeks' notice.
Clause 17 of the bill also makes provision for dismissal for garnishment. I think it is high time the government implemented this kind of legislation and I hope that other jurisdictions will follow suit. I think this legislation is an example for them and, as I said before, it is high time we ended discrimination against those who find themselves in financial difficulties, who have their pay cheques garnisheed and who prior to now were very often, if not in the vast majority of cases, fired because the employer did not like the inconvenience of having to go through the garnishee formalities.
I should like also to comment on the maternity leave provision of this bill. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). I know the interest she has in the rights of women and I share much of her concern in this regard. The hon. member has made two or three suggestions that are worthy of careful consideration by the committee. I agree with her when she said I hope I quote her correctly that the maternity leave provision and the equal pay benefits Eire real advances for the women workers of Canada.
I do not believe, however, that any piece of legislation is perfect, and I am sure there is room for improvement in this bill. Under the proposal, an employee who has completed 12 months' employment with her employer would be entitled to maternity leave of up to 11 weeks before delivery of the child and six weeks after. I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway suggested that the 12 months ought to be reconsidered and I agree with that. I also agree that perhaps there should be a degree of flexibility as to whether a person should be entitled to the leave prior to the birth of the child or after. In my experience, being the father of five children, often the real crisis is after the birth of the child and not before. This varies a great deal, depending on individual conditions including the temperament of the woman involved. There is good reason for the committee to consider this suggestion very carefully.
I am heartily in favour of the equal pay provisions. As a matter of fact, at a convention in Ottawa about a year ago, in the Chateau Laurier, I remember putting forward a resolution which was passed, changing the approach from equal pay for equal work to equal pay for similar work. It is much easier to say that someone is performing a similar function than to say it is an equal function. "Equal" implies that it is equal in every detail. I believe that if it is similar work, that is enough.
I believe that the provision for equal pay for similar work with similar responsibilities is a considerable improvement in terms of terminology and I think it will have a practical effect in terms of the relationship between employers and employees. I hope the employers will look upon this as a meaningful change and will be much more careful in the way they apply salaries to men and women in order to ensure that they are in fact equal if the work is similar.
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
In closing, may I say I strongly support this bill to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. It is a major step forward in the protection of workers in Canada under federal jurisdiction. Even more important, I think it is a great step forward by way of example for other jurisdictions to follow. I sincerely hope that the provinces will follow the lead we have given so that people all across Canada will be able to work under some kind of universal labour code which would be in their interest and the interest of the country as a whole.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, WAGES, VACATIONS, TERMINATION OF EMPLOYMENT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking of the lay-off of 500 employees by Canadian Vickers Limited, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) said this to the House on May 26, 1969, as reported on page 9040 of Hansard:
Last fall I undertook to bring this kind of legislation forward and... all parties supported me. I said on that occasion, however. that I could not visualize such legislation being before the House until late fall or early spring, and I see no reason which would enable me to advance that date.
At that time, the minister recognized that present legislation is inadequate and obsolete in many respects. Today, as we study Bill C-228 amending the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and setting up new labour standards, it would seem that the minister has at last found the spring he spoke of then, and I congratulate him.
Although the amendments introduced by Bill C-228 have long been overdue-a practice which, by the way, seems to suit this government-I am in agreement generally as to the principles involved.
None the less, as our group usually does when we find errors in a bill introduced by the government, we make whatever criticisms and suggestions that seem appropriate.
It has been a long time since the government first promised such a bill, and more specifically since the 1968 general election, and we would have expected this bill to be the result of thorough consideration. Unfortunately, in spite of this long wait, this bill is definitely inadequate. At the most, it is but the pretence of a bill dealing among other things with termination of employment and I will endeavour to limit my comments to this matter even though there are other less important issues discussed in this bill.
I will give an example in order to prove how superficial and confusing this bill is. As regards group or individual terminations of employment, clause 17 of the bill provides for the addition of several Parts, and I should like to quote subclause (4) of clause 341 of new Part I VC. It reads as follows:
Except where otherwise prescribed by regulation, an employer shall, for the purposes of this Part, be deemed to have terminated the employment of an employee where he lays off this employee.
First of all, it will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that the beginning of this clause is drafted in this way:
Except where otherwise prescribed by regulation...
5288

April 27, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
In short, when reading this bill we find that it is somehow a statement of principle or of general philosophy about the Canada Labour Code and that there is, moreover, a series of rules which hon. members may not even discuss in this House and that may very often be inconsistent with the Labour Code itself.
It is quite clear that a one- or two-day lay-off, does not come under the clause I just quoted and, to support this, I wish to bring to the attention of my colleagues subclause (d) of new clause 34K. Here is what strikes me and what should be brought to the attention of the House: no limit is set; everything will be decided through regulations.
We can see in the Quebec Labour Code that a lay-off at the provincial level cannot be final before six months.
On the other hand, under Ontario employment standards, a lay-off is considered as final if it exceeds 13 weeks out of 20.
There are other standards in other provinces.
There is quite diversity and, for sure, we can say that there is no uniformity, comparison or co-operation from one province to the other in this field.
If the minimum lay-off period which commands a notice under the proposed legislation is one week only, it is too short. However, if the minimum period is six months as in Quebec it would be too long but I will never get the opportunity to say anything about it as a member of Parliament because this period is not to be established by this House through the passing of a bill but through regulations. This system which gives precedence to regulations by putting only general provisions in the standards is unacceptable. This is often the problem with this government.
The bill we are asked to pass is high-sounding but it gives rise to injustices and doubts of all kinds and invites all kinds of interpretations. Even after a three-year study of the question, the solution is no nearer than it was before. The government bring this measure forward in hoste, a method which is more or less effective and always uncertain. In that way, the government hopes to get some support from the Canadian people and the agreement, at least in principle, of the opposition. But the legislation is so awkwardly drafted that the opposition has no other alternative then to object to details.
Unfortunately, the electorate does not realize that and it is easy then for the government to accuse us of obstruction. The opposition is blamed for not having allowed the government to approve a social security program but as a matter of fact, it is its own fault.
The young offenders' legislation was withdrawn so as to correct political as well as drafting errors.
The government organization bill was a failure, for lack of proper policy and drafting.
Today we have a major problem, although a ridiculous one, which is being met by the bill before us now. That is why, instead of a thorough account of Canadian labour standards, all we find in Bill C-228 are general ideas, many superficial things and nothing precise. For instance,-and I should like to make a detailed study of

that to illustrate my point-this is what we find in the
new section 34K:
The Governor in Council may make regulations
(b) requiring employers to comply with the provisions of this Part in respect of terminations of employment of groups of employees numbering less than fifty but greater than a number prescribed in the regulations;
Nobody knows under what conditions such a regulation could be used. There is nothing about it in the bill; the governor in council will decide that unilaterally, without consultation with Parliament. Are these estimates as those made in Ontario or are these different considerations? How many employees will be required for an employer to come under this regulation? Nobody knows.
The figure stated in subclause (b) of the new clause 34M is essential to the operation of the legislation. This is not at all a minor detail. In fact, it is important to know exactly the meaning of the word "figure". But nothing is said about it. Moreover, most labour standards in the other provinces are based on the forecast concept. Nevertheless, as regards the group termination of employment, new clause 34L provides for detrimental applications of the act and does not provide for forecast. Any notice of lay-off is probably detrimental to the employer or the employees but if we want a fair application of the law, no exemption should exist in the case of foreseeable termination of employment.
In the case of individual terminations of employment, I wonder why all employees, whatever their seniority undistinctly receive the same notice.
In Ontario, the notice period depends on how long the employee has been working for his employer. The notice depends on seniority. If he has been working, for instance, for two years, the notice should be one week. If he has been working from two to five years, the notice should be two weeks. If he has been working from five to ten years, the notice should be four weeks; if he has been working for over ten years, it should be eight weeks. It is considered that an employee with more experience is more important to the employer, and the employer because of the importance of this employee cannot fire him under such a short notice as those with less experience.
But, anyway, under the current administrative system, whether someone is experienced or not, whether he has education or not, he does not work and the bill now before us will not change his condition.
It is easier to predict the laying off of an employee with years of experience than it is in the case of a worker with little or no seniority. This procedure also seems fairer since an Ontario worker with 11 years of experience, for instance, among a group of 48 will get the same notice as if he were part of a group numbering from 50 to 200 people.
Now, under the scheme provided in Bill C-228, this man will get only two weeks' notice notwithstanding his years of service or anticipation of impending lay-offs,
April 27, 1971

whereas, belonging to a group of over 50 workers, he would get eight weeks' notice.
This is a fine example of how the government complicates its legislations and makes them incomprehensible for the ordinary worker and even for those attempting to become experts in that field.
Moreover, the Ontario Labour Code specifies that the legislation in no way alters any right favourable to the employee. But such a clause cannot be found in the standards put forward by the federal government today. Why should there be such inconsistencies between federal and provincial legislations?
Mr. Speaker, does this mean that in the case of a single lay-off, the individual laid off can claim only two weeks' notice? Is he not entitled to request a longer notice under a collective agreement or common law? If not, the standards proposed today will be prejudicial to the employee who would otherwise be entitled to a longer notice.
Furthermore, in order to make as complicated a study as the proposed legislation itself, I will say that common law provides for a notice on the part of the employee who wishes to leave his job, a notice which is not at all affected by the bill under consideration, and the required notice involves many factors, including the period of payments, the terms of employment and so forth.
At any rate, the period of notice must be reasonable- and I use here the expression of the bill itself-that is in many cases, the notice required from an employee who wishes to leave his job will be longer than that required from his employer, if the latter decides to lay him off. Such a situation is so abnormal that it must be dealt with first, but in this connection neither the minister nor his parliamentary secretary would give us any explanation.
At least, the requirements about the period covered by the notice should be the same for both sides. That is my first request to the minister. There is no reason to make them heavier for the employee than they are for the employer.
Mr. Speaker, it would be better to assure workers the period most favourable to them on the basis of seniority and, thus, on anticipation in order to recognize the rights usually granted to those who have more years of service with the employer.
We might also consider the problem of vacations. After a certain period of employment, a worker is entitled to vacations, but according to the bill now before us, the employer decides when to grant them. No provision of the present legislation prevents the employer from giving two weeks' notice to an individual, saying that the period coincides with his vacations. This does not seem to run counter to new clause 34N, because this would not decrease the rate of pay nor change any other condition of employment. This way, an employer might withhold from his employee two weeks' pay to which he would be otherwise entitled, without the employee being able to say anything against it. That is another inequity which workers cannot and should not put up with.
As for garnishment and its effect on employment, another part of the legislation deals with it. I agree
24081-54S
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
entirely with the content of new clause 34U, although its introduction is late.
There are several other things remaining and which have not been provided for in the proposed legislation. I shall deal with them through questions which I shall put very humbly and politely to the minister, in the hope that he will give a reply before the end of this debate.
First of all, what would be the effect of a strike on the notice period? Secondly, can an employer give notice to his employees while a strike is in progress, without having to pay them compensation? Thirdly, would employees having been given the required notice be allowed to strike and, at the same time, be paid by the employer, pursuant to the same act? Further, will an illegal strike be dealt with in the same way as a legal one, with regard to the notice? What will be the effect of a lock-out?
Those are important questions to which, at present, no answer is given. I do not want to take up any more of the time of the House, but I do feel that answers to those questions should be given by the Minister of Labour or his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Perrault) so that no doubts should subsist with regard to Bill C-228.
May I say that this is one of those bills which are very complicated and very difficult to understand by the worker and by the employer, both of whom we wish to protect.
It seems to me-and this does not come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Department of Labour-that those who are responsible for the drafting of bills should make an effort to simplify the text.
Being unaware of the minister's intentions, I should like to recommend to him-
